Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Labour. Would the Minister of Labour make a statement to the house, following the representations made to him by a delegation of members of parliament from the province of Quebec on March 1 last, with respect to matters pertaining to the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act and also, further, to a statement issued yesterday by Mr. Samuel Audette, director of the forestry service of the U.C.C. farmers' union, on the same subject?
Inquiries of the Ministry

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: EASTERN QUEBEC
subsubtopic: ALLEGED DISQUALIFICATION OF WORKERS
speechtext:
The hon. member was kind enough to give me notice of the question. This question was also referred to by the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) last Thursday. The hon. member for Bonaventure and a number of other members made representations to me on March 1 on this subject, which is again brought to light in the item referred to in the question as given this morning in the newspaper by Mr. Audette of the U.C.C. farmers' union. Perhaps I may be permitted to summarize that, because it clarifies the situation for all concerned.
Mr. Audette stated in this article that lumberjacks who turned down various job offers by the unemployment insurance commission had seen their payments of benefits discontinued. He also said that the jobs were turned down because the lumberjacks did not have the money to travel to localities where work was available or because the wages were below the average woodcutting pay. That is an outline of the general problem, and I can assure you that it is a problem.
When the delegation met me and the matter was brought to my attention, I asked the unemployment insurance commission to carry out an investigation to see whether any unwarranted interpretation was being made of the act against the workers, and that study and survey are being carried on.
I am assured by the commission that they hope to be able to give me ,a more complete statement on this very important matter which I may present to the house next week. In the meantime, all of the cases that are being complained about are being reviewed by the commission to make sure that the intention and the spirit of the Unemployment Insurance Act are being complied with.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROTECTION OF CANADIAN PROPERTY AGAINST CHANGE IN WATER LEVELS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROTECTION OF CANADIAN PROPERTY AGAINST CHANGE IN WATER LEVELS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 28 the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) raised a question concerning the effect of the diversion of streams into lake Superior upon the high levels of the upper lakes and whether more water could be diverted through the Chicago drainage canal.
I am informed that the range of fluctuations in the monthly average levels of the great lakes from year to year is between 4 and 6 feet. Periods of extremely high and extremely low levels do occur but not at regular intervals. Both the normal fluctuations and the extreme fluctuations are a result of natural conditions, since engineers have calculated that diversions or man-made control works in the' upper lakes influence these levels in the order of a few inches and require approximately ten years to produce their ultimate effect. Neither the water inflow at Ogoki nor any likely increased outflow at Chicago would, therefore, have any significant effect on the high levels themselves. In times of low levels, however, a matter of a few inches may be significant and, for this reason, an increase in the outflow at Chicago would reduce the general amount of water available in the lakes with results which might be prejudicial to Canadian and United States domestic and sanitary uses of water as well as to navigation interests and result in a not inconsiderable loss of electric power to both countries.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ENLARGE CLASSES OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Industrial Development Bank Act to enlarge the classes of loans that may he made under the act; to raise the limit on the aggregate amount of loans exceeding two hundred thousand dollars from fifty million dollars to seventy-five million dollars; and to make certain changes in connection with the administration of the act.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.
He said:	Mr. Chairman, the industrial
development bank has been most active on
behalf of the government and the business community since its incorporation. I should like on this occasion to put on the record some figures involved in the business of the bank and explain the proposed amendment. As I have said already, it is our intention to refer this to the committee on banking and commerce and I do not propose to engage in a debate on second reading.
The industrial development bank was established under the authority of the Industrial Development Bank Act of 1944. The purpose was to supplement the operations of existing financial institutions in providing medium and longer term credits for eligible industries when financial assistance was not available elsewhere on reasonable terms and conditions provided that the investment in the industry by others was such as to afford reasonable protection.
It was generally acknowledged that businesses, whether they were large or small, provided that they were credit worthy, had been able to raise money from their chartered bank connections for their reasonable short term or working capital requirements, and that the larger and better known businesses had not too much difficulty in raising long term funds from investors in the security markets.
It was recognized, however, that there was a gap in the lending field in that it was often difficult and sometimes impossible for small or medium-sized businesses to obtain term loans to commence or to expand their operations. The loans required tended to be too long in term to make it appropriate for the chartered banks to provide them and too small in amount to make it feasible for the borrower to go to the market with a public security issue. The government's concern was to fill this gap for an important segment of the business community and to ensure that the growth of credit-worthy manufacturing firms and certain other specified types of enterprise of small and medium size would not be impeded by the lack of facilities for adequate financing.
Section 12 (2) of the Industrial Development Bank Act required the Bank of Canada to subscribe for the authorized capital of $25 millions, all of which has been paid up. In addition, industrial development bank was authorized to issue and sell debentures not exceeding three times the amount of its paid-up capital and the reserve fund. Under this latter provision the bank had outstanding on December 31, 1955, debentures totalling $10,200,000, all of which were sold to and are held by the Bank of Canada under the provisions of the act.

Industrial Development Bank Act
The bank was authorized to make or guarantee loans or enter into underwriting agreements to acquire securities of a corporation with a view to the re-sale thereof but only if the borrower was engaged or about to engage in an industrial enterprise. A limit of $15 million was imposed on the aggregate of the amounts of all commitments which individually exceeded $200,000. This limit has been twice changed and is now $50 million. An industrial enterprise was defined to mean:
A business in which the manufacture, processing or refrigeration of goods, wares and merchandise, or the building, alteration or repair of ships or vessels, or the generating or distributing of electricity, is carried on.
Difficulties arose in many cases in the interpretation of what was and what was not an industrial enterprise, and to avoid the possibility that the bank and the board of directors might become responsible in respect of loans where the eligibility of the enterprise might be questioned and which only the courts could decide were intra vires or ultra vires, section 15(1) of the act was amended at the second session of parliament in 1949. The act now permits, and requires, the board to exercise an opinion as to the eligibility of a prospective borrower within the meaning of the definition.
From the commencement of business on November 1, 1944, to December 31, 1955, there have been 1,499 loans, investments and guarantees authorized, totalling $127,633,383, of which 254 authorizations were cancelled at the instance of the applicants before the amounts had been disbursed. These cancellations, together with reductions in the amounts of other credits before disbursements, totalled $21,011,768, leaving a net number of 1,245 authorizations totalling $106,622,115. Over the same period the disbursements in respect of loans and investments (not including guarantees where disbursements are not involved) have amounted to $99,120,538, and repayments received from borrowers have totalled $53,851,251. These repayments, with net write-offs amounting to $352,161 over the whole period, resulted in an outstanding amount of loans and investments of $44,917,126 on December 31 last. At the same date guarantees outstanding amounted to $184,237, and amounts involved in "Property Held for Sale" totalled $201,366.
Five hundred and forty-seven accounts totalling $39,901,580 have been repaid in full, and $14,722,319 has been received in partial repayment on loans which are current. These repayments, together with the write-offs for losses of $352,161, which I have mentioned, make up the aggregate of $54,976,060 by which the original authorizations have been

reduced. The remaining net authorizations on December 31, 1955, numbered 698 and amounted to $51,646,055. The difference of $6,343,326 between these net authorizations and the aggregate of the balances outstanding on December 31-$45,302,729-is represented by the amounts of authorizations awaiting disbursement. Nearly 60 per cent of the number of loans made were for amounts not in excess of $50,000.
Up to the end of its last fiscal year on September 30, 1955, after writing off $355,101 in losses (of which some $3,000 has been recovered since September 30) and after providing a reserve for losses of $700,000, the bank had transferred $7,384,259 to reserve fund in accordance with the provisions of the act.
While I am sure that hon. members will agree that this is a commendable record, the resolution which is before you for consideration has as its objective what I consider should be non-controversial improvements which I am convinced will enable the bank to render assistance to a broader field.
Prominent in the changes we are proposing is a new definition of eligible borrowers. This is designed to cover a large number of operations which under the existing definition were borderline cases or clearly ineligible. No type of business which hitherto has been eligible is omitted from the new definition but, unfortunately, no definition we have been able to devise will eliminate borderline cases. The proposal will, however, considerably enlarge the field of eligible businesses. Some examples are that businesses which were not engaged in manufacturing or processing but which required buildings or investments in machinery or equipment for assembling, installing, overhauling, reconditioning, altering, repairing, cleaning (including seed cleaning), packaging, transporting or warehousing of goods, were not eligible borrowers but will be under the proposed definition. This is also true of the businesses of logging, operating a mine or quarry-but not prospecting, wild-catting, or developing-drilling, construction, engineering, technical surveys, or scientific research or the transportation of persons. On the premise that the bank should be able to finance the same fixed assets that it would be financing if they were directly owned by an industrial enterprise, it is proposed that those who supply such fixed assets to an industrial enterprise under a lease, contract or other arrangement, whereby title to the assets is retained by the supplier, should be entitled to apply for financial assistance in the same manner as an industrial enterprise.
Section 15 (1) of the present act requires that in every case the board must express an

opinion as to eligibility, the non-availability of credit from other sources, and the amount to be invested by others. One effect is that even for an application for a loan of a very small amount the officials of the bank must submit it to the board for authorization. A practical example is that a business in, say, Vancouver applying for a loan, even a very small loan, must await the result of the submission to and action by the board in Ottawa notwithstanding that in the judgment of the chief officer of the bank in Vancouver, who would have to recommend the loan in any event, the business is clearly eligible as a borrower and that because of his knowledge of the applicant and of the available security he considers the risk, if any, to be good. It is common practice in the chartered banks to give limited and defined authority to managers of their branches, and the change now proposed would enable the board to authorize the chief officers of the bank to express the opinion as to eligibility, the non-availability of credit from other sources and the amount to be invested by others and thus up to moderate amounts fixed by the board to make credit available without the prior approval of the board.
Another amendment would enable the bank to purchase or otherwise acquire, with a view to the re-sale thereof, stocks, bonds or debentures of a corporation from a shareholder of the corporation, in addition to the authority it now has to do so, directly from the corporation. This change, it is felt, may in some cases enable the bank to extend assistance which other available security would not justify.
We also propose to raise the limit on the aggregate amount of commitments exceeding $200,000 from $50 million to $75 million. The bank's commitments for loans of this size on December 31, 1955, amounted to $24,513,445 distributed amongst 47 accounts. It is not intended that there will be any change in the policy of the bank, which will continue to be to give particular consideration to the financing problems of small enterprises, but with changes which have taken place in the complexity and cost of modern machinery and buildings, it is felt that provision should be made to ensure that the bank would not be prevented from making its assistance available in desirable cases by reason of the present limit on such loans. With lending resources now approximately $130 millions and with commitments which do not exceed $200,000 totalling $27,132,610 on December 31 last, it will be seen that there will be ample room to provide for all of the smaller applications the bank is likely to receive.
Industrial Development Bank Act
The remaining amendments are of a minor character and for the most part deal with administrative matters.

speechtext:
I have listened to the minister's statement with a great deal of interest -really more interest than I had expected- because the changes that are proposed seem to me more far-reaching than might be expected from the nature of the resolution.
The minister has recalled to our minds the circumstances of the origin of the bank. It was just at the end of the war, at a time when we were all concerned about the state of employment that was going to arise after the war.
As the minister has said, the bank was designed to meet situations which neither the chartered banks nor the bond issuing houses could easily meet. I think that his explanation there was clear. One comment that readily occurs to one is that at a timp when the minister's instrument, the Bank of Canada, is cracking down on bank loans and following a pretty tough policy of restriction, if reports are correct, we have here a provision whereby a considerable amount of new money can be created by the action of the Bank of Canada; in other words, fresh money, inflationary money unless the inflationary effect is counteracted by other policies of the bank.
When extensions were made before, for instance, in 1952 when the $25 million figure was raised to $50 million, the minister then gave us a very clear and explicit reason for the change which was being made. He referred to the fact that there was a special problem with the air transport companies and that the extra lending power was designed for that purpose. At that time I think that explanation was readily accepted. It was not a time such as we have now of tremendous activity elsewhere, not the extreme activity that we have now anyway, and that went through without question.
I am glad that the minister is proposing to refer the measure to the banking and commerce committee because it does seem to me that this great broadening of powers, which comes somewhat as a surprise, is something that we should scrutinize very carefully. We want to be sure that the government is not extending this beyond what is reasonable. In the 1952 extension the minister's predecessor carried our judgment, I think, because he referred to this special kind of enterprise which I believe carried certain definite hazards and which appealed, I think, to the common judgment of members of the house.
The explanation at this time which the minister has given sounds, superficially at

Industrial Development Bank Act any rate, much more like a spreading out and a competing with the existing financial institutions to a degree which may raise questions. One thing surprises me. The minister has indicated the extent to which the lending power has been availed of up to now. He has referred to the balance sheet of the bank as at the end of 1955, and while I have not done the mental arithmetic to figure out how much lending power is still left in the bank I think it is very substantial indeed. We can get that later in the afternoon when we come to questions. It will be some tens of millions of dollars, in fact, several tens of millions of dollars. Therefore I am a little surprised that at this stage and with all that lending power still left the minister has felt it necessary to come to ask for this further power. It would suggest a very wide, perhaps even far-ranging, extension into business which might tempt one to question it. At any rate, we can ask about that later in the afternoon.
The progress of the bank to date has been substantial but not rapid. I was surprised that in the last year the bank's loans, if I remember right, have increased less than $2 million. That is a small amount. If we question the actual operation, the number of loans made, the staff of the bank, the expenses of doing business, I think we shall find that it is a pretty expensive operation. As I say, its progress has been slow, and I would think there is a very considerable onus on the minister when we come to questions to satisfy us that this is really necessary.
I am not overlooking what I believe to be the fact, that before a loan may be made under the act

I should like the minister to listen to this-there has to be a statement by the borrower that he has tried to get money elsewhere and could not. I realize there is a certain protection there, but I do feel that we should watch carefully. We will be interested to see the details of the extensions proposed. The minister has referred to some very important lines of business, logging and so on, and when we get the bill we will have the whole situation before us.
These are the general considerations that arise in my mind. I will have questions to ask the minister, but having expressed my general thoughts I think I had better take my seat now, allow others to join in the discussion and await my time for asking questions later. I repeat that we have had this organization in operation for ten years. I think it was established with virtual unanimity. When the extension was made four years ago I noticed that there was little, if any, criticism because at that time we felt the bank was undoubtedly filling a gap which otherwise might not have been filled. In our

Mr. Chairman, unlike the hon. member for Greenwood, I am not so much surprised that the powers in the resolution are larger than he anticipated as I am surprised that they are not a bit larger than they are and that the government has not decided to take advantage of the legislation to develop an institution which might do some of the things that have been proposed in the house this session and outside of it to meet some of the needs of our economy.
Since the session opened we have had in the house proposals for federal-provincial development of power, proposals for a national plan of conservation and development and proposals for decentralization and re-establishment of industry in other parts of the country. Just a week or two ago I came across a statement by the governor of the Bank of Canada which led me to believe that perhaps the Industrial Development Bank amendment we were going to have would be of a much more far-reaching nature than it actually is. The statement appeared in the Ottawa Journal of February 27 in a report of an address by Mr. J. E. Coyne, governor of the Bank of Canada. In addressing a joint meeting of the Canadian and Empire Clubs Mr. Coyne said that he meant that the savings held by life insurance companies, trust and loan companies, credit unions, pension funds and others should be channelled into a greater flow of such funds into common stocks and other forms of equity investment. He said that it would mean more Canadian savings invested in "growth" projects rather than in traditional fixed interest investments.
Mr. Coyne did not suggest any way in which this channelling could take place. As a desirable development in our economy he merely postulated that instead of such a very large proportion of Canadian savings going into careful, safe, fixed interest investments more of them should be channelled into the type of projects in which foreign investors have been engaging in Canada of late.
In the report the other day of a speech made by an eminent Canadian statesman I noticed that he took a rather dubious view of the rise of United States investment in our growth or developmental enterprise. I have here a statement of the United States direct investment in Canada from the years 1946 to 1954. It indicates that we are experiencing

in Canada a serious development in which control of our most profitable enterprises, the enterprises that are most important in our national development, are coming into the hands of those who are not citizens of this country. I think we can view that situation with some alarm without being accused of being chauvinistic in any way or antiAmerican. I think it is an extremely serious situation when those who are not citizens of the country manage to gain control of such a large part of our economy.
I note here that the rate of inflow of United States capital in Canada has been rising extremely rapidly in the last five years. In 1950 it was $243 million; in 1951, it was $309 million; in 1952, $363 million; in 1953, $372 million. Then in 1954, when we had what I see is now admitted to have been a recession, United States investment dropped to $346 million. That was the gross inflow of capital. The net inflow of capital, however, has been ranging in the neighbourhood of $350 million for the last several years.
We are sometimes told-indeed we were told it in this house not long ago-that we have to welcome this United States investment in our Canadian development because the Canadian economy is not capable of supplying the necessary capital. Many persons accept that statement at its face value and say, "Oh yes; Canada is a poor, poor country. We ain't got no money". But when we look into the figures of Canadian assets, we realize that an entirely different picture is the true one. Mr. Coyne states that a certain amount of the pool of capital in the control of life insurance companies should be directed to equity investments in the development of Canadian resources. When we see the figures for 1953-which are the last complete figures I have been able to get-and when we note that the total assets of insurance companies were $5,568 million, we realize that there are vast sums of capital in Canada.
It is interesting to see how those sums of capital are invested by those who have the responsibility for their investment, namely the life insurance companies. In many instances, of course, they are constrained by legal restraints as to the fields of investment they may go into. The life insurance funds are invested to the extent of over 60 per cent in bonds and debentures, and 23 per cent in mortgage loans. Only a small percentage- about 10 per cent of their total assets-is invested in either preferred stock or common stock or equity investments. The assets of the life insurance companies have been increasing at an enormous rate in recent years. In 1951 they amounted to $4,880 million. In 1952 this amount increased by almost $400
Industrial Development Bank Act million to $5,207 million. From reports that I have seen-they are not official reports but they are reports that I have seen in the financial press-I believe the assets of the life insurance companies today total well over $6 billion. Presumably the investments are carried on in much the same proportions as those I have read out.
With regard to the other institutions in which Canadian capital accumulates, we have the loan companies. The loan companies have total assets-and this is again as of 1954-of $253 million. Again we find that the large proportion of it is devoted to investment in bonds, debentures or in real estate mortgages and agreements of sale, and largely in agreements of sale. The percentages are: Mortgages, 70 per cent; bonds and debentures, some 20 per cent. Again only a small proportion-4-79 per cent-is invested in stocks or in equity holdings in development enterprises.
Trust companies are in much the same position, having available funds, as of 1954, of $139 million. Again nearly 50 per cent of this amount is invested in bonds and debentures of the Canadian government, provincial governments and municipal governments. Only 1-3 per cent is invested in stocks or equity holdings.
If we in Canada are going to combat this tendency or trend-which in my opinion is a rather dangerous one-in our economy of the valuable, profitable and economically important investments in resources development falling into the hands of people who are not citizens of the country, then we must take some decisive steps to channel those investments into other fields. That is my reason for being surprised that the government has not taken advantage of this legislation or of this amendment to set up the industrial development bank in that role. It is all very well for us to speak in general terms and say that our Canadian capital should be invested in this field or in that field, that it should be channelled here or there. But unless we set up some instrument for accomplishing that objective, we are of course merely talking to the wind. One can rest assured that those who are in control of these pools of capital know very well what are the best and safest investments for the funds that are entrusted to them and that they are not going to change their fields of investment merely as a result of exhortation. Hence I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that had the government seen fit to expand the powers of the industrial development bank, particularly in the field of the issuance of debentures, to a much larger extent than they are at present permitted, much of these funds might have been channelled into the industrial development bank


industrial Development Bank Act and have been made available for loans to those who are engaged in the development of our resources.
The debentures and bonds of the industrial development bank should be as attractive fixed-interest investments as any others, and might very well attract a sufficient volume of funds at the disposal of life insurance companies, trust companies and loan companies to offset the present $350 million to $400 million annual investment of United States funds in the development of Canadian resources. Sometimes I think we forget the process by which these United States investments are made. We perhaps forget that there have been Canadian citizens who have made certain discoveries and have required financing for their development. From these tables that I have been reading, it is perfectly obvious that the ordinary sources of funds for such development are not readily available in Canada from the traditional lending institutions. We have heard a great deal about risk capital, but apparently Canadian capital has an extremely strong aversion to taking any risks. The first thing we know is that a United States Company has decided to undertake this very development that has first been mooted by a Canadian. In reading over the reports in Hansard of 1944 when this bill was first introduced into the house I noted that there were members of parliament at that time who considered this step to be extremely dangerous, indeed to be a socialistic innovation. I refer to the setting up of the industrial development bank. It was apparently going to lead us down the path to complete socialism. I would suggest that it has signally failed to do that, and that it has not even functioned to the extent it was expected to function.
Never at any time has the industrial development bank been operating at the capacity of the existing legislation. At the moment it is operating at about half capacity. It has a lending capacity of approximately $100 million but has less than $50 million out now. This is, of course, partly because of the restricted fields of investment to which it was confined but it was also because for a number of years since 1944 the development of Canada was subordinated to some extent to the provision of arms for the Korean war and the provision of defence installations for the cold war. But since 1950 the tempo of development in Canada has increased enormously. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that if we wish to preserve the Canadian economy primarily as a field for Canadian investment and Canadian opportunity, then the government must take some steps to see that we proceed in that direction.


1 would urge the Minister of Finance to seriously consider adding to his amendment an amendment which would increase the powers of the industrial development bank to issue debentures and to increase their capital stock to permit that, so that they would have on hand funds for development investment to equal or at least approximate the funds which are now brought in from across the line. Only in that way are we going to cope with the problem that more and more Canadians are viewing with increasing alarm.

It will be my privilege, Mr. Chairman, to again disagree with the hon. member for Greenwood, as I have done so often, and approve of the minister's move to expand the activities of this bank. I see no reason, Mr. Chairman, why we should not develop this bank into something corresponding to the Reconstruction Finance Corporation of the United States. It seems to me that Canada acts altogether too helplessly and babylike for a nation of her economic strength and population. She does not seem to have enough courage to get up and do anything in a financial way to help herself. This institution could easily be developed into an institution through the use of which we should not sit around on a log and sigh because United States capital does not come in fast enough to develop our oil resources, our gas resources or build our pipe lines or do any of the many things that need to be done in Canada. We shall manage to do these things for ourselves, just as we undoubtedly have the capacity to do. I, therefore, heartily approve of the minister's move in expanding this act. My only disappointment is that he has not expanded it nearly far enough. I think if he had doubled the activities, capacities and powers of the bank this year, he would not have gone recklessly forward in his efforts.
Now, that is the first comment which Social Crediters would make, and I believe all factfacing people would take that attitude. We come now to this matter of inflation once more. We find the hon. member for Greenwood contributing to the delinquency of Canadian public opinion by trying to convey the absolute falsehood that what we are in at the moment is an inflationary period. He knows, and he has heard time and time again, that the increase in prices from which we now suffer were the direct result of the increase of $5 a ton in the price of steel in April, 1946. Will the hon. member rise and say he does not know that? If he does not know it, will he write it down somewhere in his notebook so he cannot forget it. He knows certainly that in 1946 the steel workers struck for their share of the $5 increase,

thereby increasing the wage rates all across Canada. Certainly he has enough intelligence to know that such a performance in our Canadian economy would result in an increase in price all across the board! Why in the name of common sense does the member get up here and time and again try to delude the Canadian people into thinking that this manipulated rise in prices from which we are suffering is inflation? I just cannot understand the mentality of the hon. member for Greenwood and so many of the people who are in behind him.

I am not opening up, Mr. Chairman, a general discussion; I am pointing out how absolutely fallacious the remarks of the hon. member for Greenwood were when
Industrial Development Bank Act he made objection to the expansion of the powers and functions of this bank; that is all. How could an extension of the activities of this bank, as is proposed in this resolution, possibly result in inflation when we have three or four different conditions existing in Canada which are anything but inflationary, namely substantial unemployment; surplus goods of every kind; we have extensive credit buying, indicating there is a shortage of purchasing power, and we have a tremendous amount of resources which are not being used.
In the face of those four conditions, how could anyone maintain that the expansion of money through this industrial bank is going to cause inflation? I will say no more at the present time about this aspect of the question. I simply state that no fact-facing individual who is desirous of giving the truth will object to the enlargement of the powers of the bank on the ground that it may cause inflation. That would be the second general observation of Social Crediters.
The next one is simply that something must be done to prevent the influx of United States capital into Canada to buy shares in our productive enterprise. I wonder whether the government really intends to give this country to the United States. I wonder whether government policy is definitely designed to get Canada so deeply in debt to the United States that she will come one morning and take us all over. We are permitting a vast accumulation of United States capital, as the hon. member for Nanaimo pointed out, to go on, with nothing being done by Canada to offset that, to produce Canadian capital with which to buy our own enterprises and develop them, thereby preventing so great an influx of United States capital. I would say that this move to expand the activities and the powers of this industrial development bank is a move designed to prevent in a measure the enormous use of United States capital in the development of Canadian industry.

I see no reason why money should be borrowed by this institution with which to carry on its activities. Mr. Chairman, we certainly have wonderful opportunities here to take courses in economics, which cram in all the very different points of view in the course of a very few minutes.
I find myself just a bit on the horns of a dilemma in connection with how I feel about this resolution. I think it is well-known here that members of my party and I are strong advocates of the free enterprise system. I heard someone say "what does that word mean?" I, of course, understand that it is a word that a lot of people dare not pronounce at all, but it is one that I still feel I can use without any fear. It may be that in this particular instance the people who might have made sure that this type of help was available to industry may have overlooked the possibilities.
I believe the real reason for the legislation was to cover the gap which existed under our banking system and that which existed in the United States. Under the legislation in the United States the banks are quite entitled -the terms of reference under which they operate-to take security on real property as a method of giving loans. In this country, of course, that is not possible. Under section 75 of our own Bank Act, subsection 2(c), we find that our banks are not permitted to lend money or make advances upon the security, mortgage or hypothecation of any lands, tenements or immovable property. I know there is one exception to that, which is set out under section 79(1), under which they are entitled, under certain circumstances, to take mortgages of that kind as additional security. But generally speaking, the rule precludes them from making use of that kind of security. That restriction is not apparent under the United States legislation,

and as a result the average industrial borrower is able to get pretty good coverage as far as his financial requirements are concerned. When I speak about the average borrower, I am speaking about the smaller businessman. When we get up into the class referred to by the minister, the people who are borrowing $200,000 or more, in most instances they are able to go out and get a financial house somewhere to float their debentures, and are able to get the help they need. If I understand the amendment in this connection, it will tend to increase the help in that category, but I do not see it becoming any more available, as a result of this particular amendment, to those who are borrowing smaller amounts of money.
I am wondering why the chartered banks did not recognize this need, or shall I say this opportunity of getting into this type of investment. I do not think it was because they had not sufficient funds to handle this type of investment. Their most recent statements to the end of January this year indicate that the total amount of loans made by this government institution might be described as peanuts in so far as their total assets are concerned, and their ability to handle this type of transaction.
I want to give the same word of warning I gave last year when we were considering an item similar to this. If these institutions do not see the necessity for handling this type of loan, if they do not come forward at the time when assistance is needed, then they cannot complain if this government moves into every phase of business. I should think therefore that we might say to those institutions that this gap still exists. They are the people who have the facilities to handle this type of loan from one end of the country to the other.
I think this is one of the weaknesses in the industrial development bank set-up. We get their brochures every year and they indicate that they have only four offices across the country. That may be all right for those who are borrowing large sums of money and the necessity of travelling several hundred or a thousand miles to one of the offices would not be something to overcome them, but the small businessman who may want to borrow $25,000 or $35,000 has this hazard placed before him and there would probably be some reluctance to take this trip to see if he could borrow money. I think the total number of loans that have been made under this legislation offers concrete proof that this type of financing is not being made available to the people who really need it.
Then I think there is another restriction upon the use of the facilities of this bank. This is really an internal matter in so far 67509-122
Industrial Development Bank Act as administration is concerned. I do not know whether the minister is moving to correct this, but he has indicated that greater responsibility may be given to the regional people in accepting applications for loans. I think it is ridiculous to place a limit of $5,000 on an application that may be accepted by someone who is acting in a supervisory capacity over one-quarter of the country. At the present time applications for greater amounts must be submitted to the head office. There are also time-consuming delays in connection with the administration of this act, and these should be eliminated for the benefit of the borrower who is at the stage where he needs money and needs it in a hurry.
I think the minister said something about the board of directors not having to approve in certain instances, but I think he should move to correct a situation where various people who are acting in a supervisory capacity in one part of the country or the other are going to find themselves in a position where they have no discretionary power at all in the case of the ordinary type of loan.
I know that it is a characteristic of the chartered banks that limits are placed upon the discretion of their managers, but it should be remembered that these banks have branches in almost every town and hamlet in the country and it is much easier for someone to go to a branch to make an application and then have it sent forward for approval.
In considering this particular problem I am reminded of the speech made the other day by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris who had moved a resolution about the decentralization of industry. If we are going to have true decentralization of industry there should be decentralization of the facilities of this bank, which was created for the purpose of ensuring that industry could get the type of assistance it needed.
If we are going to provide these facilities, let us make them available to the smaller groups of people; let us see that they are available to the smaller communities. They should not be concentrated in just a few offices. I see that the office in Montreal has jurisdiction right through to Halifax. The office in Toronto has jurisdiction from Montreal to Winnipeg. Then there is an office for the west and another one for British Columbia. If this bank is to fulfil its true role there should be additional offices opened in order to make its facilities available to other people.
I want to say that the amendment made previously has done a remarkable job in the air transport field. It has enabled the development of air transport to remote districts

Industrial Development Bank Act by companies whose opportunity to borrow was limited because of the type of flying they were doing. It has enabled pioneering companies of this type to obtain assistance which would not have been available otherwise.
I have only one other observation to make. I notice that this bank does not pay corporation taxes. The other day one of the hon. members to my left argued that it should not be necessary for certain types of government institutions to make a profit, but it seems to me that if we are going to avoid socialism in the use of this particular type of institution we should expect this institution to face the same industrial and business hazards that we expect any other person carrying on any type of business or banking to face.

I submit that the operations of this bank should be carried on the same as those of any other type of business. They should be ready to face the same hazards and be able to come back here and show a profit.
As they do not have to pay corporation taxes I suppose it could be assumed that those who borrow probably get a better deal than the fellow down the street who has to borrow from another institution which must show a profit for its shareholders. However, I think generally those institutions are able to show a profit and still operate on the same basis as institutions which do not have to show a profit.
These are observations which I think should be made at this time. If the facilities were extended to provide greater access for the smaller type of businessmen, then I think this would provide a greater future for the employees of this bank. I think there is a tendency in a great many cases with institutions of this kind that their employees get to a certain level and their opportunities then disappear. As a result we find that we lose a great many well qualified people from these institutions to other places in the economy. If we are going to use this type of thing, let us see that it benefits not only those who are borrowing. Let us see whether it can be made to give some benefit to those who spend their lives doing this work.

In the preamble of the annual report of the industrial development bank I notice a portion of a sentence that refers to the objects of the bank. It says that one of its objects is with particular consideration to the financing problems of small enterprises.
The industrial development bank, I take it, was organized to provide a means of granting assistance to small enterprises. It was meant to be a means of sustaining and developing the so-called free enterprises of the dominion. However, when we look at the statistics released recently by the Department of Trade and Commerce and see the economic outlook for 1956, telling us that next year we can expect the sum of $7,500 million to be invested in Canadian enterprise, and when we look at the amount that is being supplied by the industrial development bank to small enterprise, and we realize that this year it was less than $13 million, we come to the conclusion that the government of Canada has very little faith indeed in the solvency of so-called small enterprises.
Small enterprises in Canada is the only type of free enterprise that we have, and I have regretted to see so little assistance available-$13 million out of $7,500 million-[DOT] to small enterprises. Large enterprise is able to get all the money it needs in the money markets of the nation and, if it is unable to get it here, as in the case of the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines, it then goes south of the border and is able to add to the amount of money available to it. I am quite prepared to grant that a large share of this $7,500 million that is going to be invested next year is being invested by the federal government, the provincial governments, the municipal governments and other local bodies such as hospital boards and so forth. However, the fact remains that nowadays there is oodles of money available for municipal, provincial or federal government enterprise. There is oodles of money available for huge private enterprise. There is very little money available in the nation for small enterprise; and I regret this.
In looking at the distribution of the little money that is available to small enterprise, I regret that, of the $12,700,000 that I believe was loaned by the industrial development bank last year, almost the whole of this money went to that section of industry that was engaged in manufacturing. The industries engaged in providing services received very little money indeed. The hon. member for York West expressed his appreciation of the money that was available to one service industry, for the expansion of air services. However, I believe that if he will look at the record he will see that thus far, out of

the $104 million worth of loans made, the air services received slightly over $3 million, a niggardly percentage. I see that the refrigeration services received only a little over $5 million.
If we look at the list of individual enterprises given on page eight of the report, we note that almost all of the money that was available was made available to manufacturing industry. You had to turn out a product, sr your application was almost automatically laid aside and you were declared ineligible. For example, I know the case of a man in southern Manitoba who erected a cleaning plant. These cleaning plants for the cleaning of seed grains are becoming popular across the prairies. This man found, after the completion of the building and the installation of some of the necessary machinery, that his estimate of the costs exceeded his estimate of the funds he would have available, and he applied to the industrial development bank for a loan. He received a very abrupt reply to this effect: "You are a man of good character; your investment in this enterprise will be much higher than the minimum standards laid down. However, because you do not manufacture a product, you are ineligible for a loan." I think that is regrettable.
I think our investment in Canada in enterprises of additional productive capacity is high enough. It is time we called a halt and applied the brakes to this ever-continuing investment to add to the productive capacity of the nation, the ability of the nation to produce more and more of the goods which we already cannot sell and for which we cannot find markets. More of the available resources of our nation might be devoted to investment in the provision of services.
I regret, for example, that more of the funds are not made available for investments on the part of our Canadian municipalities. I feel that amendments might very suitably be introduced whereby the industrial development bank might be used as an instrument to help municipalities to finance self-liquidating projects.
I am not advocating that money be made available to municipalities for the building of sidewalks or any other non-self-liquidating project. However, I think that such things as the municipal distribution of natural gas, electrical energy and municipal water services could very well be financed through the industrial development bank.
I regret that the industrial development bank is not operating to its authorized capacity. I believe it is authorized to make loans to a maximum of $75 million. However, I see that total loans outstanding at the present time only amount to some $44 million.
67509-122i
Industrial Development Bank Act Only a little over half the money available by law to the industrial development bank has yet been made available to Canadian industry. In my opinion the policies of those charged with the responsibility of administering the act are far too conservative. When we look at the record of the losses that have been suffered I think we will have to agree with the statement that the operations of the bank have been on a far too conservative basis. Last year their write-offs were only $37,000 out of an interest income on loans, investments and guarantees of $2,193,848. Looking at the whole history of the bank, we see that since November 1, 1944, it has had interest income-I should like to emphasize the word "interest"-of $12,329,626 while losses only amounted to $355,101. I think that in itself is sufficient evidence to convince anyone that the industrial development bank has not been taking its fair share of risk and has been overly and ultra conservative in its policies. The losses are small.
I believe that another reason why the bank has not been utilized even to the degree now allowed is that the services of the bank are, relatively speaking, unknown to those who have the greatest need of the bank. I think it can be fairly said that there is hardly a multimillionaire in Canada who does not know of the services available to the Canadian people through the industrial development bank. I think it is fair to say that there is not a member of the house or of the other place who does not know of the services available through the industrial development bank. However, as I go about the country I find that very few of the small enterprisers, and these are the only free enterprisers, have ever heard of the services made available by the parliament of Canada through the industrial development bank. I think a lot more energy might well be devoted to making the services that are available known to those who need the services and for whom the services were meant in the first place.
In glancing at who are responsible for the administration of the act and the names of the board of directors from across the country, I fail to see a single representative of the small enterprisers of our nation. I see a goodly number of men who are responsible for some of our major Canadian enterprises and who, if and when they need money, are easily able to obtain it, as are their associates, in the money markets of the world. We have our government bodies to whom money is available by the floating of bonds and debentures. We have our multimillion dollar corporations to whom money is available in the money markets of the world. However, in the case of those owning small

Industrial Development Bank Act enterprises money for capital expansion is often very hard to get, and in my opinion there should be some representative on the board of directors of those for whom the services of the bank are meant.
We had a resolution the other day concerning the decentralization of industry in Canada. I intended at that time to say a word on the decentralization of the biggest industry in the country, the government of Canada. Among other things that I meant to mention at that time, and I am going to mention it now because it is applicable here, is that in the list of supervisors of the bank I see the name of Mr. N. C. Tompkins, 475 Howe street, Vancouver, B.C. Mr. Tompkins is supervisor for the whole of Alberta, British Columbia, the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. The bank is intended to aid small enterprises, and I do not believe that a man stationed at 475 Howe street, Vancouver, has much knowledge of small enterprises in the northern part of Alberta. I think it is time that the government decentralized its own affairs. If the industrial development bank is supposed to help small industry, its operations will certainly have to be decentralized to a much greater degree than to have one supervisor responsible for as vast a territory as Alberta, British Columbia, the Yukon and the Northwest Territories.
As I mentioned before, I am concerned about the conservative policies of the bank as evidenced by their very small losses. I should also like to add that I think the bank is too conservative in that it provides only some of the debt capital and none of the risk capital of Canadian industry. I believe it could perform a valuable national service if it turned some of the United States capital invested in Canada from the risk capital category to the debt capital category. As far as I can ascertain, the industrial development bank is only willing to enter into the debt capital field and enters the risk capital field only to the extent of surplus funds on hand. I think that policy is wrong and a lot could be done both in the interests of Canadian industry and the national welfare of the country as a whole.

Having said that, Mr. Chairman, I should like to deal with one or two further points on this bill. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam made one point which I find here in my notes and on which we certainly find ourselves in agreement, namely the need for this industrial development bank to make itself better known to the small business men in Canada and to sell its services to that group in our economy. In a few moments I shall make reference to the rather weak job which has been done in that particular field by the bank. But I would point out that nowhere in their operating statement for the preceding year do I find any item whatsoever representing advertising or a sales effort of any kind on the part of this bank. As the large commercial banks move ahead and as they quite properly expand their operations and make their services better known to the Canadian public, it seems to me that a similar function might well be performed by the industrial development bank. As one example of the public relations work which is being done in this field by the other banks, I need only cite the monthly news letter published by, for example, the Royal Bank of Canada, the Bank of Montreal and the Bank of Nova Scotia. Those documents play an important part in influencing Canadian business men and in making them conversant with various matters. While I certainly do not counsel a tremendous expenditure on publications by the industrial development bank, nevertheless, since it is apparently going to have even more to do as the result of this bill which is to come before us, I would hope they would make an increased effort to let the small business men of the country know of the availability of their services.
Now, I would refer for a moment, Mr. Chairman, to the composition of the board of directors of this industrial development bank. It is an interesting fact that one-third of the board of directors come from Ontario,

Industrial Development Bank Act five out of the 15, and two out of 15 come from Quebec. The remainder of the board is composed of one member from each province in Canada. When I set that against the loans being made by the bank I found a surprising discrepancy. For example, taking the current authorizations at September 30, 1955, we find that while Ontario has one-third of the directors, businesses in Ontario have borrowed only some $19-6 million out of a total authorization for all parts of Canada of $67 million. Against that we find that Quebec, with only two directors, has borrowed $26-4 million, substantially more than Ontario. And then, we find that British Columbia, with only one out of the 15 members on the board, has had authorized for the use of businesses in that province some $11-6 million. It would seem to me that there is a substantial discrepancy between representation on this board of directors and the activities of the bank in Canada. While I have no doubt they are all fine and estimable men-I see a number of them are members of the public service of Canada, which makes them doubly estimable, I have no doubt, in the view of this house as in my own view-I would hope that some consideration would be given to dividing this one-third group from Ontario and distributing directorships somewhat more widely across Canada.
Again, the point has been made that the bank tends to work most heavily in the field of large loans, that is large loans for it. But 1 do not think anyone has yet made the point this afternoon of just how evident that is, because some 50 per cent of its total current authorizations at September 30, 1955, were for loans of $200,000 or over, whereas for loans of under $200,000 they only had the remaining 50 per cent of the bank's authorization. Admittedly many more individual firms were represented by smaller loans, but even there there was only a total of 632 firms with loans of $200,000 or less. In the real small-business class, with loans of $25,000 or under, there were only 240 firms that currently enjoyed the benefit of this banking service. I, for one, would be very happy to see the extension of the bank's activities more heavily in the field of the small borrower, the man who most needs this help, rather than in the field of the large borrower.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COSTS, LICENCES, REPAYMENT, ETC.
speechtext:
The
minister has indicated, Mr. Speaker, that it is his proposal that this bill be referred to the banking and commerce committee. Because of that, and since we have already had a debate this session on a public bill on the subject of small loans, and because we had a debate last year on the subject of small loans with respect to a similar bill, I propose to be quite brief. I know also that this particular bill has been in circulation for some time and has had fairly widespread comment throughout the country.
Last year, in connection with the debate on the bill proposed by the hon. member for Assiniboia I made some reference to the work of the parliamentary committees in this field in 1938 and 1939. My remarks are contained in Hansard of last year in the debates of May 6 and May 27. I do not propose to repeat illustrations of the points of view of the parliamentary committees again today. I do think, however, it would probably be appropriate to summarize the aims and objectives of past parliamentary committees by quoting from a brief that was submitted to the government last summer by the representatives of lenders in the small loans field. Amongst other things they gave the parliamentary committee this credit by saying:
In the words of the chairman of the House of Commons banking and commerce committee,-
That is the committee of 1938.
-"throughout its inquiry your committee's objective has been to secure the best procurable rate for the borrower".
That is the end of the quotation of the words of the chairman of the committee at that time. The brief of the lenders in this field went on to say:
In fact, the entire report of the House of Commons banking and commerce committee presents an excellent analysis of the basic problems inherent in providing consumer loans.
The two-fold purpose of the legislation was:
1. To protect the borrowers against exploitation by unethical and illegal lenders.
Small Loans Act
2. To provide a regulated lending service on a broad scale at a rate sufficient to provide an adequate supply of capital to meet the need.
The Small Loans Act does not apply to banks; it does not apply to pawnbrokers, and it does not apply to lenders whose charges do not exceed 12 per cent per annum. It does not apply to loans that are made beyond $500. The act stipulates that lenders of between $1 and $500 who have in mind a charge in excess of 12 per cent per annum must obtain a licence, must report to the Department of Insurance with respect to their business transactions; and interest and all other charges in connection with the accommodation to the borrower must not exceed 2 per cent per month.
The volume of business in this field has grown rather impressively. In the first year of our supervision, namely 1940, I believe the total volume of business was about $20 million. It is expected that in 1955 the volume will be not quite but almost ten times that amount of lending.
As I have indicated, at the present time there is no regulation with respect to lending over the amount of $500. Our statistics and information as to the extent of personal loans that are made in the field above $500 are not too complete. However, the licensed lenders who lend in the field under $500 do apparently supply to the Department of Insurance information as to the extent of their business in the field over $500. In addition to that, one of the large lending companies in Canada lends exclusively in amounts over $500, and information as to their business is available. And then, of course, there is known to be lending for which there is no report. But we do know there has been a great and rapid development in the amount of money that is being lent in the nature of personal loans in the field over $500.
Our information is that generally licencees under the Small Loans Act who lend both with respect to amounts under $500 and over $500 generally charge 2 per cent with respect to loans over $500. There are a few of the licensed lenders who charge less than that. We know of one or two who, in this unregulated field, charge more. And of course we have heard from time to time of unlicensed people who charge much more than the 2 per cent, which is the amount stipulated under the present Small Loans Act for loans under $500.
The association of licensed lenders have themselves indicated that, because of excessive charges sometimes made by unlicensed lenders in the field above $500, it appears now that it might be desirable to have a higher ceiling for the Small Loans Act. The
1S36

Small Loans Act
bill with which hon. members are familiar proposes that the ceiling be raised, that the government regulation be raised from $500 to $1,500.
If the scope of the act is increased from $500 to $1,500, I think it will be obvious to all hon. members that it would be inequitable and undesirable to maintain the same maximum interest or cost rate for the large loans that is now provided for relatively small loans. Thus the bill proposes that there be a graduated interest or cost rate, and it is proposed in the bill that the rate be 2 per cent on any part of the unpaid principal balance, not exceeding $300, plus 1 per cent on any part of the unpaid principal between $300 and $1,000, plus-if the loan is beyond that-one-half of one per cent per month on any remainder of the unpaid principal exceeding $1,000 up to the proposed ceiling of jurisdiction, which is $1,500.
In considering the propriety of a rate of this kind, hon. members might be interested in some of the rates that are applicable in the United States at the present time. When our act was introduced in the late thirties the regulated ceiling was set at $500, a higher ceiling than was generally provided in most of the states of the United States, which at that time was $300. Having regard to the fact that it is equitable to have a rather lower maximum rate with respect to a large loan in relation to a small loan, our maximum rate was rather lower than generally prevailed in the United States at that time because our ceiling was $500 instead of $300.
I find that the situation at the moment is that in the state of New York the charges under their small loans act are 2\ per cent on lending for the first $100; 2 per cent between $100 and $300, and one-half of one per cent between $300 and $500. They do not take jurisdiction under their small loans act beyond a ceiling of $500.
In the state of New Jersey the rates are 2\ per cent up to $300; one-half of one per cent from $300 to $500, with the maximum loan under their regulations being $500.
In the state of California the rate is 2J per cent for the first $100; 2 per cent between $100 and $500, and five-sixths of one per cent between $500 and $5,000. It will be seen that they have a very high ceiling of jurisdiction, namely $5,000, which I believe is the largest in the United States.
In the state of Pennsylvania the rate is 3 per cent on the first $150; 2 per cent between $150 and $300, and 1 per cent between $300 and $600. They have a ceiling of jurisdiction of $600.

In order to give a comparative effective rate of interest in relation to the proposed maximum rates in the present bill and those charged in the states of New York and New Jersey, which I have indicated, the figures would be as follows: If the loan were $300 the charge under the rates recommended in the present bill would be 2 per cent; under the New York legislation the rate would be 2-26 per cent; in New Jersey the rate would be 2-50 per cent.
In the case of a loan of $500, which is the maximum of jurisdiction in those two states, the effective rate of interest under the present bill would be 1-81 per cent; in the state of New York it would be 1-88 per cent; in New Jersey, 2-12 per cent.
The bill recommends that the rate of interest or the rate of maximum cost will continue to be expressed as an all-inclusive percentage of the amount of funds loaned. This was the recommendation of the parliamentary committee of 1938, and I think it is generally the practice in the small loans field in the United States.
The bill contains a prohibition against the splitting of loans. Hon. members will realize that when the maximum rate of interest is on a graduated scale, being less for the larger amounts, there might be a tendency for a lender to exert pressure on an applicant for a loan to divide his application, a portion to be advanced to himself and a portion probably to his wife. As a consequence there would be a higher over-all rate of interest on a split loan provided to the lender. That is being legislated against in the bill.
As I have explained, the definition of cost of loan at the present time is quite embracive and includes practically all possible costs that might be involved in connection with a loan of this kind. However, it has come to our knowledge that in recent years lenders, particularly in the United States, have to a growing degree been asking borrowers to take out insurance policies, and the cost of the premium is an extra cost to the borrower. There has been little experience of that happening in Canada, although some lenders have voluntarily provided life insurance or other forms of insurance in connection with their loans for their own better security. The bill will provide that if an insurance policy is considered desirable by the lender the cost will be included in the definition of over-all cost to the borrower.
The present act provides with respect to overdue loans and loans for rather long periods that the rate of interest will revert from the maximum of 2 per cent to 12 per

cent per annum. A rate of 12 per cent per annum works out legally and technically at [DOT]95 of 1 per cent per month. Hon. members will realize that this is an awkward arithmetical calculation for all concerned, and it is proposed in the present bill that when 12 per cent per annum is referred to it will be 12 per cent per annum payable at the rate of 1 per cent per month, which is a much easier figure for arithmetical purposes.
Notwithstanding the Small Loans Act, the Money-Lenders Act is still in existence. I think that act was originally passed in 1906. For all practical purposes it has been superseded by the Small Loans Act. The continuation of the Money-Lenders Act is confusing to most persons and since its effectiveness is practically nil the present bill proposes to repeal the Money-Lenders Act.
In order to provide time for necessary investigation of lenders not presently licensed but who would become subject to the act, and also to enable licensees to make all necessary changes in practice, it is recommended that the amendments come into force on January 1, 1957.

Mr. Speaker, this is a bill to amend the Small Loans Act, 1939. At the time the original bill was introduced the banking and commerce committee went into the matter fully and there is a report in the proceedings of the committee for that year. In 1946 the situation was reviewed and changes in the interest rates were considered but were not recommended. The banking and commerce committee report of that year again indicates a full discussion of the subject.
This business is of substantial size, as is indicated by the fact that in 1954 the number of small loans made was 831,721. It should be pointed out that conditional sale and hire-purchase agreements where merchandising and loan transactions are included in the one transaction, do not come within the purview of this act. The reason given is that constitutionally this is a provincial matter. No doubt this question can be carefully looked into when the banking and commerce committee meets.
As I have said, we approve of a review of the operation of the act and will vote to have it sent to the banking and commerce committee. In doing so we are not committing ourselves to any particular rate *of interest 67509-123

I wish to express my appreciation to the parliamentary assistant to the minister for his very comprehensive review of this field in introducing this important bill. I welcome the proposed bill and the proposed amendments contained in it. I think it is a demonstration once again that parliament can be effective.
There is a view held in some quarters, which we hear expressed from time to time, that if a member of the opposition should propose a resolution or a bill, he automatically spells the doom of the proposition he advocates, and nothing can come of it. That would be rather a bleak attitude to take of this parliament and of parliamentary democracy if because a member of the opposition sponsored something, the government would automatically oppose doing anything about it.
There are, of course, many instances in which members of the opposition have proposed public bills or resolutions which the government, in fact agreed to adopt and put into legislative form. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) proposed and subsequently obtained amendments to acts that would prevent stoppage of pension rights to persons because they had gone on strike. The hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) proposed a year or so ago that red wrapping should be removed from packaged bacon, and the government accepted that proposition.
I could go on and name other instances. The hon. member for Kamloops proposed that crime comics be abolished, and that suggestion too was adopted by the government. Other instances could be mentioned. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, advocating that all medical expenses should be deducted from income for taxation purposes, was able to get the government to agree to reduce the 4 per cent provision to 3 per cent.
This is another of those instances where a proposition sponsored by a member of the opposition has found at least a measure of support on the government side of the house. Because of the general agreement among many members of different parties in the house and because of general support throughout the country, it has resulted in steps being taken to improve existing legislation. I am happy over the part I had to play in this field. able to do so is that the government allows them to charge such excessive rates of interest.
People go to their offices to borrow money in large measure, I believe, because of the high pressure advertising campaigns put on by these companies. They spend enormous sums of money for advertising. The two companies to which I referred spent almost $1 million in the same period for advertising purposes alone. While the parliamentary assistant has pointed out, and quite correctly, that they pay almost half their exorbitant profits in corporation taxes, I want to point out to him that the Department of National Revenue allowed these companies I am sure I am correct-to charge the whole $1 million against expenses for income tax purposes.
Because they are able to charge in that way this very large sum of money spent on advertising, they on the one hand deny the Canadian government substantial revenue and on the other hand-and this is the more serious part of it-engage in advertising that is definitely misleading to a great many potential borrowers. You hear this high pressure advertising over radio and television. You see it in the streetcars and in the newspapers. Do you want to borrow any money? If you are in any kind of trouble go to one of these small loans companies. They are not going to ask you any embarrassing questions. They have a credit manager with a wonderful personality who would just love to see you. Come on in and talk over your business with him. You will not have any trouble. You will not have to sign too many documents. It will be a very simple transaction. We will do it on a personal basis, and the costs are very moderate.
They do not mention the interest rate. They do not mention the fact that their charges are excessive. As a result many people in need of small loans go to the small loans companies; and when they do they must, of course, pay these exorbitant rates of interest. The fact that the small loans companies spend 40 times as much on advertising no doubt accounts for them getting so much business.

people who are good substantial risks. I have no doubt that would include almost everyone who is interested in obtaining a small loan because, as I have already pointed out, the rate of loss in this field is very small indeed.
