subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COSTS, LICENCES, REPAYMENT, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad that Bill No. 51 is to be sent to the banking and commerce committee. When that bill is before the committee I believe we should investigate not only the question of consumer credit but also that of merchandise credit, because today merchandise credit is playing a larger and larger part in the sale of commodities.
When the question of small loans was before the banking and commerce committee back in 1938 I recall that we made an exhaustive study of the whole question. We had before the committee representatives of the credit unions, the small loans companies, the Canadian Bank of Commerce and many other financial institutions. One thing of great interest was that at that time we also paid attention to the relationship between merchandise credit and consumer credit.
It is interesting to note what the committee reported on that question in their third report. I should like to quote from page 418 of the report of the committee of June 1, 1938:
The practice of mass-production resulted in a pressure for mass-consumption, with a widely advertised acceptance of "a small payment down and the balance on easy terms". Thus a large load of modern debt is in the form of unpaid balances for goods already consumed or in the process of consumption. These debt charges do not come directly within our reference or, for that matter, do they ordinarily come within legislative action; while legislatures have everywhere meticulously concerned themselves over debts incurred by borrowing money, legislatures have not shown equal concern over debt incurred by the purchase of goods.
Whatever the legislative distinction; in practice, there is a relationship between merchandise-credit and money-credit that cannot be safely ignored in prescribing the rate of charges in borrowed money. A strict comparison of the rates of merchandise-credit with cash-credit is difficult, if not impossible, largely because the cash price of goods so often bears a portion of the credit-cost.
However, it is safe to say that the two branches of consumers' credit are to some extent interchangeable. Upon evidence submitted to the committee, some of the money loaned at rates exceeding 2 per cent a month was borrowed to effect reduction in payment for goods, especially to avoid penalties under instalment plan of payment. And evidently there is a wide variation in the rates of charges involved in instalment sales. The committee was told that rates as high as 186 per cent per annum had been paid by Nova Scotian fishermen in the purchase of fishing equipment on six months' credit; while on certain household equipment the rate involved in instalment sales is about 12 per cent per annum.
Small Loans Act
Well, if that was true in 1938 I think it is probably even truer today, because we know that buying on the instalment plan and by charge accounts has become quite a big business in this country. 1 think, therefore, it would be very wise for the banking and commerce committee to spend some time investigating that situatibn and perhaps make recommendations regarding it.
The proposed amendments in this bill are improvements to the act in regard to the definition of costs, in regard to interest rates and in regard to the amounts of the loans that can be brought under the act at specified interest rates. But unfortunately this bill will not help the majority of the small loans borrowers, because the majority of the loans made under the Small Loans Act are for less than $300. For instance, I quote from one of the pamphlets put out by one of the large small loan companies, Household Finance Corporation, entitled "Consumer Finance in Canada". On page 5 it states:
In Canada, there are now over 165 household offices in cities and towns from coast to coast. These offices make over 600,000 loans annually, in sums up to $1,000. Sixty-eight per cent of the loans are for sums of under $300-
Now, 68 per cent of all their loans are under $300, and those borrowers will not get any help at all from this bill because they will still be paying 2 per cent per month interest. I think most of us will agree that in all probability these borrowers of small amounts are just as much in need of assistance as some of those who borrow larger amounts. I believe we should try to set a straight rate of 1 per cent per month on the whole of the first $1,000. I realize, of course, that the cost of making loans in small amounts is higher, the overhead is higher, but on the other hand the rate of 1 per cent per month is approximately 13 per cent per year and that is an exceptionally high rate. I believe that a rate of 1 per cent per month or 13 per cent per year should be sufficiently high to cover the loans made under the Small Loans Act, even if you had to average the costs in order to get a fair rate.
As has been mentioned by the hon. member for Assiniboia, the average rate charged by the Canadian Bank of Commerce in 1954 was 10-46 per cent. I believe if it is possible for the Canadian Bank of Commerce to get on satisfactory with a rate of 10-46 per cent, it should be possible also for the small loans companies to get on with a rate of 13 per cent. This would allow them a slightly higher rate than the Canadian Bank of Commerce in order to meet their requirements. I know it is often said that it is a different class of borrowing; the people who go to the small loans companies' are the people who are not

Small Loans Act
sufficiently creditworthy to get loans from the Canadian Bank of Commerce. But of course that is not true. The reason the very large percentage of people go to the small loans companies instead of the Canadian Bank of Commerce is that they want privacy. If they borrowed from the Canadian Bank of Commerce they would have to get an endorser or perhaps two endorsers. They do not like to do that, and they are prepared to pay a higher rate rather than get an endorser. It is not merely a question of privacy. I think we all realize the position of anyone who has to go to another individual and ask him to guarantee his loan at the bank. Consequently they go to the small loan companies and pay a higher rate.
Now, since the amendments to the Bank Act in 1954 the chartered banks are able to take chattel mortgages. It may be possible for the Canadian Bank of Commerce and other banks to make loans through the personal loan branch without insisting upon an endorsement, in a similar way to the small loans companies. But there are many loans made under the personal loans branch that are unsecured. I have been informed that 40 per cent of the loans made by the personal loans branch of the Canadian Bank of Commerce were unsecured, and 29 per cent of those made by small loans companies were unsecured. The cost on this type of loan would be less than for a loan that had to be secured by a chattel mortgage.
Then another reason people go to the small loans companies is due to what you might call the high pressure salesmanship exerted by the large amount of advertising that is carried on. I believe that is one place the small loans companies could cut down; that is the cost of their advertising. The point is that this may be due partly to the fact there are too many small loans companies operating in Canada. When you increase competition beyond a certain point it actually has a tendency to increase costs.
I was not certain of that point myself, but I was very much interested in the discussion on an insurance bill that took place before the banking committee the other day. Mr. MacGregor told us that if too many companies got into the field in competition with one another it actually increased the cost of advertising and increased the cost of insurance to the purchaser. If that is true of insurance I should imagine it would be true of the small loans business. If you get too -many people in the field making small loans there is an increased amount of advertising necessary, and that unnecessarily increases the cost to the borrower.
[Mr. Quelch.l
I notice there has been quite a large increase in the small loans companies operating in Canada recently. In a report on small loans companies and moneylenders by the superintendent of insurance for 1954, we find this on page 6:
In my report last year, I referred to the greatly increased interest being manifested in the small loans business in Canada by established lenders outside Canada, more particularly by those with head offices in the U.S.A. Several of these lenders entered the field during 1954 through provincially-incorporated subsidiary companies and the same trend has continued up to the date of this report.
It seems strange to me that if the net profits of these small loans companies are so small, it is claimed down around 2 per cent, that so many more companies should be set up. Two per cent is not a high rate of profit. I cannot imagine a profit of 2 per cent encouraging the setting up of additional small loans companies. The suggestion that some of these companies are operating at 2 per cent is fantastic, but I have seen that statement in some of their advertising.
You have only to pick up the report of the superintendent of insurance and turn to the pages of balance sheets to find that their profits have been very much greater than that. The amount of the reserves and the amount of capital reinvested in the company is shown. You have to take the amount of profit reinvested in the company in order to ascertain the true picture of these companies. I think the mere fact that we have so many companies flocking into this country shows they are making a pretty substantial profit.
Now, I am not satisfied that a rate of 1 per cent per month or approximately 13 per cent a year would put the small loans companies out of business. I believe they could reduce their costs in many ways. They could certainly reduce the cost of operation by cutting down on a lot of their advertising. We have all received in the mail recently what I would call a very expensive type of advertising. One needs only to walk along Sparks street and Bank street to realize that almost every other building is plastered with the signs of small loans companies. One would come to the conclusion that Ottawa must provide a very profitable source of income for small loans companies, because I have never seen as many small loans company offices in any town as apparently are operating in the city of Ottawa.
Then I imagine they could take a lower rate of interest on the profits they themselves have reinvested back in their companies, and they could take a lower rate of profit generally. I am satisfied that these three things alone would make it possible for them to operate on a rate of 1 per cent a month.

I believe the government should also approach the chartered banks for the purpose of trying to get them to take a greater responsibility in the field of personal loans. Apparently up to 1954, the Canadian Bank of Commerce was the only bank that had entered seriously into the field. No doubt when this bill is before the committee we shall be able to find out what action has been taken by other banks since the amendment to the Bank Act permitting chattel mortgages.
It seems to me that at' the present time banks in this country are becoming altogether too prone to lean upon the government. Any time there is any risk involved they appear to want the government to guarantee them against loss. Of course any time the government guarantees them against loss, and pays part of that loss, it is subsidizing the banks. Surely the banks of Canada are in a sufficiently strong position to be able to stand on their own feet without everlastingly wanting the government to guarantee them.
In view of the great concessions the banks do get from the government of this country, I think as a service to the country they should be prepared to enter more and more into the personal loan field.
Then, of course, there is another class of people who have no credit or little realizable wealth. These people would not be considered credit worthy. They would not be able to borrow from the banks. It is very doubtful whether they would be able to borrow from any small loans company. Their only hope is to go to some welfare organization such as the Red Cross for help.
As time goes on the government will have to give consideration to setting up some kind of an institution to help the really down and out individual. It stands to reason that a person who is in a very difficult financial situation would probably have very little chance of borrowing from a bank. He would be forced to go to a small loans company-the amount of the loan could be small-and pay 2 per cent per month interest. He is the very last type of individual who can afford to pay 26 per cent interest a year. Those are the people who really need help.
I hope further consideration will be given the matter, to try to find ways and means of making credit available to those people at a low rate even if it means some sort of additional guarantee to the banks for making these loans.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COSTS, LICENCES, REPAYMENT, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no legislation which I have welcomed more since the opening of this parliament than this legislation. In my opinion its general tenor indicates reform
Small Loans Act
legislation at its best. It is an endeavour tc legislate in the best interests of the average Canadian citizen.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, there is a prevailing opinion today throughout the country-and 1 think it is a sound one-that loan companies and finance companies have been making excessive profits at the expense of the average Canadian citizen. This bill is designed tc correct that state of affairs. Even at the reduced rates it is my opinion that the loan companies can make a fair and reasonable profit. Hence sufficient money will still be available for those people who wish to borrow, and who are not able to meet the rather high standards of the chartered banks. Since they will still toe able to borrow money, they will not be thrown into the waiting arms of the loan sharks.
Let us briefly consider how small loans are made available today. First of all we have the chartered banks; second, we have the credit unions; and third, the small loans companies. With regard to chartered banks, hon. members know that personal loans are available at the rate of 6 per cent. As the result of legislation passed in 1954, the banks are now able to take chattel mortgages as security. Whether or not this has appreciably increased the number of loans granted by the chartered banks is not as yet known. We should have that information fairly soon.
Of course, as the hon. member for Assini-boia has mentioned, the Canadian Bank of Commerce has gone into this field; but some of the other banks are reluctant to do so because they feel they cannot charge more than 6 per cent, and they cannot add those different services to the basic amount of the loan. In other words, Mr. Speaker, it is a matter of interest. If the banks could charge, say, 12 per cent for small loans I believe they would go into this field more readily. Of course that brings up the most difficult question which I think was considered a year or so ago by the banking and commerce committee. No decision has been reached.
Again, I suppose, the bank is: more interested, on the present basis of 6 per cent, in lending money to finance companies, and they in turn lend it to the public.
With regard to the second form, namely credit unions, as the committee which investigated this whole problem in 1939 said, credit unions can remain effective only with homogeneity in social, religious and economic relation. That is to say, they are confined largely to special circumstances, although I admit they are prevalent in certain parts of this country, particularly the caisse populates in the province of Quebec, where they are doing

Small Loans Act
an excellent job. I understand they usually charge 1 per cent a month. However, no credit unions pay income tax.
Finally we come to the Small Loans Act, the small loans companies and the moneylenders.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COSTS, LICENCES, REPAYMENT, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at six
o'clock I was saying that in 1939 the banking and commerce committee dealt with the Small Loans Act, and subsequently parliament passed that act. At the same time the MoneyLenders Act was in force. Actually it seems to be an anomaly because only four companies were subsequently incorporated under the Small Loans Act, including two of the largest small loans companies in this country, Household Finance Corporation of Canada
[Mr. Hollingworth.l
and Personal Finance Company of Canada. Actually most of the small loans companies have been incorporated under the MoneyLenders Act. As far as I can find out the terms of the two acts are pretty much the same.
The rates of interest provided were 2 per cent per month as a maximum up to 15 months, and then 1 per cent per month subsequently. As I say, at present there are only four companies which were incorporated under the Small Loans Act, but 61 companies have been licensed under the Money-Lenders Act. The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance told us this afternoon that the Money-Lenders Act is to be repealed. I think that is a rather good idea, because confusion is apt to result unless one reads the two acts together.
As hon. members are well aware, the terms provided by the bill before the house are 2 per cent per month for loans not exceeding $300; 1 per cent per month for loans exceeding $300 and not exceeding $1,000; and half of one per cent for loans exceeding $1,000. I should have mentioned that under the old act the ceiling for small loans was $500, but under the bill we are considering this evening the ceiling will be $1,500.
At the outset may I say that I am certainly not accusing the small loans companies of sharp practices. I think in general they have shown integrity in their dealings with the public, but with respect I do question their good taste and wisdom in their high-pressure advertising. Certainly one is made aware of their advertising. There was a song popular not so long ago that ended with the words, "I owe my soul to the company store". The first two or three times I heard that song I thought Tennessee Ernie was saying, "I owe my soul to the finance co."
There certainly are usurers who are willing to live off the avails of destitution, if I may use the colourful phrase used by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), during the debate last year in a speech which I enjoyed very much. Certainly I am not accusing the finance companies of this, nor indeed did the hon. member for Peace River; but I do submit that an attempt has been made on the part of some finance companies to entice the unwary, the unwise and the timid into their counting houses there to be despoiled of their financial independence.
Particularly, Household Finance Corporation have used the slick, glossy pap of the typical supercharged United States huckster, much to the distaste and annoyance of the average Canadian. The Household Finance Corporation blasts forth over the radio every morning in Ottawa the merits of their loans.

That is all well and good, but when one lives in Ottawa during the session and has to hear this every morning it does become rather annoying.
We are interested in the profits made by small loans companies, and for this information we go to the report of the superintendent of insurance for Canada dealing with small loans companies and moneylenders. I believe this was referred to by the hon. member for Assiniboia. I should like to refer to the report for the year ended December 31, 1954. This report is interesting for the information it provides, but it is interesting also because of several omissions which I should like to point out to the house.
For example, only those companies registered under the Small Loans Act or the Money-Lenders Act are referred to. In other words, if a company does not make any loans under $500 there is no record of it in this report. I found that there was a very interesting reason for this. I hear it stated over the radio that Household Finance Corporation makes loans from $50 to $1,000, but on perusing this book I found no reference to any loans over $500.
There is a section which deals with other small loans companies and moneylenders, which indicates the volume of loans made other than small loans. In other words, I find nothing under Household Finance Corporation for loans of more than $500. Upon looking into the matter further I find that there are two companies. There is the Household Finance Corporation of Canada which lends up to $500 and does business under the Small Loans Act, and there is Household Finance Company Limited which makes loans of over $500. Unfortunately there is no record of that company in this book. [DOT]
As I say, we are interested in the profits made. I notice that for 1954 the profits of Household Finance Corporation of Canada operating under the Small Loans Act were $5,952,000, or practically a cool $6 million. It is true, as someone mentioned this afternoon, that out of that would have to come a considerable amount of income tax, and naturally they pay dividends to their shareholders. But I think we will all be ready to admit that the profits were considerable.
Now, if we may go to the other large small loans company, Personal Finance Company of Canada, we find that their profits amounted to $923,000. The interesting part about this is that the report deals with the profits of Personal Finance Company of Canada from loans of more than $500. Those profits are indicated as being $2,500,000, or two and a half times as much. Therefore if we project
Small Loans Act
this result into the results of Household Finance Corporation, if we multiply their profits of $5,952,000 by 2-6, we come up with profits of about $16 million. I am not saying that Household Finance Corporation made that much money, but I do say it shows that this is a most lucrative business.
I think the government has done a wise thing, something which will be appreciated by Canadian people from coast to coast, in bringing this reform legislation before the house. In view of the profits indicated I do not think the finance companies are going to suffer if their interest rate is reduced to 1 per cent.
There is one other thing I should like the house to consider, but I suppose I would be out of order in discussing it. This has been brought to my attention by my constituents and other persons. I think the larger acceptance corporations or discount houses should be brought under this legislation. I do not suppose we can do that, but I think that is one of the next problems we will have to face.
In any case this bill is going before the banking and commerce committee, where it certainly will be studied exhaustively. One interesting point to consider is whether the ceiling should be raised to $2,500. Hon. members will recall the very able speech by the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Brown), that genial member from southern Ontario, in which he made a very good case for an increase of the ceiling to $2,000. I took note also that in the very able presentation by the parliamentary assistant this afternoon he pointed out that in California the ceiling was raised to $5,000. That is something the committee can carefully study when the bill goes before it.
Again, should the rate be 1 per cent right across the board? I should think there are cogent reasons why that should be considered. Or, again, should the ceiling for the 2 per cent per month be reduced to $200? Once again, the committee will have to determine that.
At this stage I should think that we would need to have more evidence on these points, but I want to make it very clear that I am supporting the general principle of the bill. I am sure that after the committee studies this bill an act will ensue which will incorporate the best features, will provide justice for the Canadian citizen and, at the same time, will enable the finance corporations tG enjoy a reasonable and fair return in their business. After all, they are legitimate business concerns in a free competitive society.
I take great pleasure, therefore, in congratulating the government, and particularly

Small Loans Act
the Minister of Finance, on their foresight in bringing in this bill and on their practicality, which at the same time is strongly tempered and imbued with social justice.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. Boss Thatcher (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre):
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COSTS, LICENCES, REPAYMENT, ETC.
speechtext:
I had not intended to speak on this subject until this afternoon, when I heard my old friend and colleague the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) make his remarks.
The subject we are discussing, of course, is charged with emotion. Every hon. member, I am sure, regardless of his party would like to make sure that the working people of Canada can borrow money at the lowest possible rates. Yet it seems to me that parliament must take great care that in adopting arbitrary interest ceilings it does not force these companies in the small loans business to take their capital elsewhere and invest it in some other field.
In the year 1954 some 800,000 Canadians borrowed money from small loans companies. Most Canadians from time to time get into financial difficulties. If such a Canadian happens to be an employer, usually he can go to the bank and use an overdraft. But for working people usually this is not possible. In such cases they invariably go to a small loans company and make a cash loan. I think real hardship will follow if parliament, either indirectly or inadvertently, makes it impossible for people in the working class and in the lower income groups to get capital from those companies.
I certainly approve of government regulation in this field. I think everything possible should be done by parliament to eliminate sharp practices. Everything possible should be done by parliament to make sure that excessive and unjust interest rates are not charged by these loan companies. But I also think we should not forget the economic facts of life.
Today in Canada there are thousands of places where any company can invest its funds. Therefore I say again, let us make certain that our legislation is not restrictive to the point where these companies take their cash out of the small loans field and invest it somewhere else. Let us be sure that we do not prevent people in the lower income groups from obtaining urgently needed credit.
To illustrate the danger of this, I should like to remind my hon. friend from Assiniboia and my other C.C.F. friends of an act which the Saskatchewan government passed some 11 years ago. It was called the Saskatchewan moratorium act. During the depression years we had a great many farm foreclosures by mortgage companies in our province, and many of these foreclosures were unjustified. So the C.C.F. government, in good faith and (Mr. Holltngworth.]
with good intentions, introduced legislation which in effect prevented the mortgage companies from foreclosing on the home quarter section. I supported the legislation, and I thought it was sound at the time.
Unfortunately it has not worked out that way. For those who had already borrowed money and did not need any more, it was wonderful. They did not have to worry, even if they could not make a payment. However, the contrary was true for those who needed money in the future. The mortgage companies, feeling that they had no longer security of investment in the province of Saskatchewan, moved out lock, stock and barrel. As a result, in our province today you simply cannot buy a farm on credit unless it is through the Canadian farm loan board, and those loans are few and far between. In my opinion that legislation, which as I say was introduced with every good intention, has had the effect of virtually ruining farm credit in Saskatchewan.
So I say tonight, let us as members of parliament benefit from this example and make sure that we do not achieve the same results with these small loans companies. I think there should be no illusions. These people must be allowed to make a reasonable profit if we expect them to remain in the field. It is up to the banking and commerce committee to go into this whole question, study it carefully, and then decide what is a legitimate and reasonable profit. Personally I have always contended that parliament should give greater encouragement to the banks to get into the small loans field. But if we want them to do this we are going to have to permit them to charge interest rates that are more in line with what we permit the small loans companies to charge.
I remember that several years ago Mr. N. J. McKinnon, general manager of the Canadian Bank of Commerce, appeared before the banking and commerce committee. He stated that at that time, under existing laws, it simply was not feasible for the banks to enter extensively into the small loans business. The interest rate the banks are able to charge today is 6 per cent. That works out on a monthly basis to about 10-46 per cent. Mr. McKinnon told the banking and commerce committee that if the banks could charge 1 per cent per month, he was reasonably certain they would go into the small loans business more extensively.
So I suggest, Mr. Speaker, before you rise, that this might be a point for the banking and commerce committee to investigate. I think if the banks were to enter this field the small

loans companies would be forced by competition to lower their rates, and then it might not be necessary to do so much by legislation.
I repeat, let us approach this whole problem, not emotionally but realistically and sensibly, in an endeavour to give all working people the lowest possible interest rates. But let us not wake up and find that we have low interest rates, but no money available for loans.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat referred to the danger of capital being taken elsewhere, that is out of the lending field, if interest nates are made too low. I am glad he also coupled with that a desire to have all the facts placed before the committee, because in the report of the operations of small loans companies as of the end of December, 1954, there are some figures which show the position of some of these companies.
I shall not weary the house by going through the whole list, but I think this one will serve as an example, and I think it might allay the fears the hon. member may have as to the danger of the capital of this company going into another field.

speechtext:
I have the report of Household Finance Corporation of Canada as of December 31, 1954. It is shown in their balance sheet that while they have an authorized capitalization of $5 million the actual capitalization is only $3,070,000. On that capitalization they have outstanding balances at this time of $55,495,730.52, and their total assets now stand at $57,783,971.94. Even more interesting and significant is their revenue account. Bearing in mind that their total paid up capitalization is only $3,070,000, we find that their income earned on loans for that year came to $12,758,246.95. Added to that we have recovery of bad debts, doubtful accounts and disposition of some office property, which gives them a gross income for the year of $12,812,433.21.
Further down their expenditures are shown, and taking them off we find that their gross profit for that year came to $5,952,743.75 on a total capitalization of $3,070,000.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COSTS, LICENCES, REPAYMENT, ETC.
speechtext: Before income tax.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COSTS, LICENCES, REPAYMENT, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, before income tax. I doubt if a company that can make a gross profit of almost $6 million on a total capitalization of $3 million are going to feel that they will want to take their capital elsewhere to a different field. The parliamentary assistant to the minister has interjected, "before income
Small Loans Act
tax." In order to satisfy his mind on that point, let us go to the dividend account. Of course dividends are not paid until taxes are paid. We go down further and find that dividends to shareholders in that year came to $3,048,510, and on a capitalization of $3,070,000 that is just a wee bit short of 100 per cent, almost dollar for dollar in the form of dividends.
I can assure the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre that any commercial company that can pay its shareholders every year a dollar in dividends for every dollar they have invested is not going to take its capital elsewhere and look for a better investment unless, of course, they are exceedingly greedy. I would not want to accuse even this company of being in that category.
I doubt that the bringing down of interest rates generally as visualized by this legislation or as advocated by the members of the C.C.F. group over the years constitutes any danger so far as availability of capital is concerned for the small loans business. Not only that, but we find in looking at the statistics that the number of small loans companies is increasing very rapidly. The amounts they spend on advertising their business come to a tremendous figure. Such companies do not increase in number, nor do they put on a high pressure advertising campaign, if they are in a field which is not profitable. The fact is that they do spend huge sums of money on advertising, and while I would not say their advertising is dishonest it is not very far from being dishonest and is certainly misleading in the way it is put. For that reason I do not share the fear expressed by my hon. friend that this type of legislation, or the type of legislation envisioned by the hon. member for Assiniboia, would constitute a danger tc the availability of this kind of money.
I want to refer also to the remarks of the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Holling-worth). If I heard him correctly this afternoon, and I speak now subject to correctior because it was a little difficult to hear at tha1 time, he said that credit unions do not paj interest. If that is what he said, and that i: the way I understood him, of course I wil have to say that he is quite mistaken. Credl unions do pay interest, and they do a grea deal more than that as far as the people the; do business with are concerned. They provide life insurance at no extra cost to those wh< make use of their facilities. They also provide loan insurance, so that if the person whi borrows money from the credit union is no able to repay the loan because of death, dis ability or some other reason the loan i written off as provided in the bylaws of tb

Small Loans Act
credit union. In the case of death the life insurance is, of course, payable to the beneficiary.
Therefore the credit unions are providing a service which is not comparable at all to that provided by the private small loans companies. But the chief difference between the operations of the credit unions and those of the small loans companies is the fact that the credit union is a non-profit organization. That in itself is a very important difference which sometimes is not recognized by the government.
Not so many years ago we had occasion, when discussing an income tax amendment, to try to impress upon the government the fact that co-operative institutions generally and credit unions in particular are non-profit organizations and therefore should not be treated in the same way as private companies for income tax purposes. We were not altogether successful, although we did persuade them to some extent.	*
The reason I bring that into the discussion at this time is that the hon. member who has just taken his seat referred to the desirability of the government providing encouragement to the banking system to get into the small loans field. I should think it would be far more desirable all around that if encouragement at the government level is to be made available, it should be made available first of all to the credit unions. Because of the nature of the credit union, which is a nonprofit organization, it does the most for the community in which it operates, not only for the people who invest their money directly in the credit union or make use of its lending facilities but also for the community generally, because every dollar that goes into the credit union remains in the community. None of that money goes to the headquarters of a huge company outside the province or sometimes outside the country, as is the case with the small loans companies. Every dollar circulates within the community.
They charge an interest rate of about 1 per cent per month, and when they have completed their fiscal year they sit down and draw up their accounts. If they find that the amount of interest money is more than is required for their general operations, they then divide the surplus in two ways, either in paying a certain amount in interest on the money that investors have placed in their credit union for the purpose of lending, or by reducing the interest rate to those who have borrowed money, or both. Therefore when they have a surplus at the end of the year the result is that the interest rate is much less than 1 per cent per month, because a rebate is made to the borrower in 
so far as it is possible to do so in order to give him the best possible break.
But the important thing to remember is that the money invested in the credit union, money that is circulating in the community' is left there for the purpose of building up' the community. None of that money is siphoned off in the form of profit to go outside the community, outside the province or outside the country. Therefore if the government is inclined to give encouragement to lending institutions as a principle, I respectfully suggest that the credit unions are the best possible vehicle through which they can provide that kind of encouragement and do the most good in the community and in the nation at large.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (for the Minister of Finance) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO REORGANIZE CAPITAL STRUCTURE, INCREASE AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 84, to amend the Canadian Farm Loan Act.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. M. Benidickson (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO REORGANIZE CAPITAL STRUCTURE, INCREASE AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is an amendment to a bill that I think over the years has proven very much worth while to the farming community. Its original purpose was not especially to lend money in great volume to farmers, but it was to be a sort of pace-setter in so far as interest rates were concerned, because interest rates were chiefly in the eyes of the legislators of 1927 and 1929 when this original bill passed the House of Commons. Since that time, however, some $100 million has been lent to farmers under the terms of the farm loan act. I think about 43,000 loans have been made. In the last year of record, namely the year ending March 31, 1955, the new lending amounted to $8,200,000.
In addition to this worth-while legislation providing farm credit, hon. members are aware that since the war we have also had in operation a form of government guarantee of loans made by banks to the farmers under the provisions of the Farm Improvement Loans Act. The difference between the two acts could probably be roughly described as long-term credit with respect to the Canadian Farm Loan Act and intermediate credit with respect to the Farm Improvement Loans Act. Originally the farm loan act board was accompanied by a provision for supervising loans to fishermen. Hon. members will well

remember that last year the house passed a bill which could be described as parallel to the Farm Improvement Loans Act, namely the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. In consequence of that legislation the farm loan board will no longer be required to supervise loans to fishermen.
The bill before us tonight in summary could be said to simplify the capital structure of the farm loan board. It will simplify its capitalization, and it will also simplify the system with respect to reserves. It will broaden the board's activities by increasing the maximum amount of loans that can be provided under the act. It will simplify and improve the lending procedure by eliminating the short-term second and chattel mortgage loans, and it will dispose of the capital of the board acquired in connection with its operations under the Canadian Fisherman's Loan Act which I have described.
As the act stands at the present time, the capital of the board consists of $5 million which was originally advanced at the inception of the board, together with issued shares of stock to the amount of $2,240,301. The $5 million initial capital advance was made during the early years when the board was becoming established, and for three years it did not bear interest. But since that time it has borne interest paid by the board to the government in a manner similar to that in respect of any other borrowings of the board from the government. It is considered desirable to convert this original capital into an ordinary loan. The bill will provide for the repayment to the government of the original advance, and it is intended to refinance this repayment through an ordinary loan by the government to the board at current rates of interest.
The bill will further provide for the cancellation of the $2,240,301 issued capital stock of the par value of $1 per share, and in substitution the board will be capitalized by 30,000 shares of stock of the par value of $100 a share, the total value of which will be $3 million. With respect to reserves, under the existing statute the board has been required to set aside at least 10 per cent of its net annual earnings in a special reserve fund. This reserve is known as the "statutory reserve" and at the present time it amounts to $878,000. But this is not a reserve in the ordinary sense of the word because it has not been available, under the statute, for the payment of losses. In addition to this statutory reserve the board, under long practice, has had a special reserve built up on the basis of one-half of one per cent of its lending. This reserve now amounts to $2,349,258. In substitution fo" these two
Canadian Farm Loan Act reserves the bill will provide for the establishment of a single reserve account to which all losses may be charged, and it is stipulated in the bill that the amount of the reserve will never exceed the amount of capital which, as I have indicated, will be $3 million.
Prior to 1952 the board could raise money only by the issue and sale of bonds to the minister of finance. This was an awkward and cumbersome method of financing, and in 1952 parliament made provision for simple borrowing by the board from the minister of finance without the necessity of issuing bonds. It is now proposed to go a step further and drop the bond issuing provisions entirely, and to convert all the board's borrowings into simple straight loans from the minister of finance. The original purpose of the bondissuing power was to enable the board to borrow money directly from the public, but this was never done.
As part of the simplification of the capital position of the board, the bill will also provide for disposing of the capital and assets of the board under the Canadian Fisherman's Loan Act. Lending under that act was discontinued, as I have indicated, following the coming into force of the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. The amounts involved are not substantial but are somewhat complicated from the point of view of the balance sheet and the annual report which is submitted to members of parliament.
The farm loan board received a capital advance of $29,000, and in addition the government holds 161 shares of stock of the board of the par value of $1 each, issued respecting loans to fishermen. It is proposed that the board shall repay the capital advance and retire the stock less the operating deficit which has accrued under this act. This deficit amounts to $5,203, and will be absorbed by the government. There are still a few outstanding fishermen's loans, and the bill will provide that the proceeds will be paid into the consolidated revenue fund as and when those loans are repaid by the fishermen. When completed this will wind up the Canadian Fisherman's Loan Act operation.
So far as the lending limits are concerned -and I think this is the most important feature of the present bill and the procedure under it-the board can now lend $10,000 on first mortgages plus $2,000 on second mortgages for a shorter term. Under the present legislation the board finds it mandatory, in connection with second mortgages, to take chattel security. The bill that is now before us will eliminate short-term second mortgage lending. I have indicated to the house we have very important and worth-while companion legislation for intermediate credit in

Canadian Farm Loan Act the Farm Improvement Loans Act. This bill will eliminate this type of second mortgage for short periods, and the chattel mortgage features of it, and it will increase the maximum amount of loan under the act under first mortgage procedure to $15,000.
The bill will change also the percentage ratio of loan value. Prior to the amendment of the act in 1952 the board was not able to lend beyond 50 per cent of the appraised value. In 1952 this was increased to 60 per cent. It is now proposed to further increase the ratio to 65 per cent. It is also proposed to drop the provision for setting up an advisory board. I think the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) will welcome this statement, because in 1952 when this provision was presented he felt that it would not be a useful part of the act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO REORGANIZE CAPITAL STRUCTURE, INCREASE AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
have been interested, Mr. Speaker, in the remarks of the parliamentary assistant concerning this important piece of legislation.
I say it is important because the provision of credit to our farm population is a subject that has occupied the attention of parliament for a good many years. It was not until 1927, however, that this house took any definite action to deal with the specialized need of our farm population for a special type of credit. The original passing of the farm loan act came, I believe, as the result of pressure from the Progressive group which at that time made up a fair percentage of the representation in this house.
The general changes that have been outlined by the parliamentary assistant move in the right direction. Section 6 deals with the major changes so far as the terms of the farm loan act are concerned by increasing the amount of the first mortgage to $15,000 and also providing for the granting of a loan at 65 per cent of the actual value of the land upon which the loan is made. That is moving in the right direction. During world war II the subject of farm credit receded somewhat into the background, and also during the immediate period following world war II, when farm income was unusually buoyant. It is just in the last three or four years that organized farm opinion has begun to pay more attention to this problem, and the amendments that we have before us I am sure have come as a result of the demands from farm organizations for more generous credit provisions in the act.
At the outset of my remarks I said that the farm economy requires certain special features by way of credit provisions. In the early years the credit needs of the farmers were largely taken care of by private loan

companies which operated alone in this area up until world war I. This was particularly true during the development of the wheat economy on the prairies. However, in the boom period of world war I credit facilities became somewhat overextended, with the result that a huge indebtedness was incurred by prairie farmers. This indebtedness was still outstanding at the onset of the depression, and necessitated special adjustment legislation in order to assist the farmers in getting out from under their burden.
The first entrance of the government into this loan field came in the province of Manitoba in 1917, when the provincial government passed the Manitoba farm mortgage act. I should say that the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta followed suit very soon afterward. Unfortunately, because of inefficient management, because of the unpredictable nature of grain growing on the prairies, the wild price fluctuations and so forth, provincial activities in providing credit did not continue to function successfully beyond 1923. It was then that the agitation from the Progressives, the farm representatives, began. They were thinking in terms of the provision by the federal government of more extensive credit facilities.
Now, while these amendments are a step in the right direction, I think it is fair to state that they do not go as far as the special capital needs of our agricultural economy require. As a result of the unhappy experience of private lenders in this particular type of lending operation, the supply of capital from that source has been drying up. This means that more and more the farmer- I am speaking particularly from the standpoint of the western farmer, but I think it would apply generally-is dependent upon the sources of credit such as are provided under the farm loan act.
The parliamentary assistant indicated that this act was originally thought of as a pacesetter, encouraging lower interest rates and generally setting the pattern for the specialized needs of farm credit. However, it seems to me, Mr. Speaker, the activities of the farm loan board have today gone beyond the demands of pace-setting, and the board is in the position, because of the changing circumstances, where it is one of the major agencies for providing this kind of service to the farm population.
I say the farmer has special needs for credit. He has need for short-term credit. This is taken care of to a large extent by the banks, and by self-financing through friends. According to the latest figures I have seen on this matter, most of the short-term

credit used by the farmers comes from selffinancing sources. Also, of course, the credit union method of providing short-term emergency credit has become increasingly popular among our farm population. The real problem arises in connection with long-term capital provision. This was the basic function that the original farm loan board was established to perform.
Agriculture needs long-term credit more than any other type of business activity. The return on the farmer's investment is comparatively small and the recovery of the investment of necessity, because of this small return, occupies a long period of time. In most cases, particularly in reference to financing in the grain economy, it requires long-term financing up to a period of 40 years. Under the Canadian Farm Loan Act long-term financing is provided for up to 25 years. Therefore there is a real deficiency in this regard in the act as it stands at the moment.
Another special problem of the farm economy in regard to credit is the necessity of providing capital at the lowest possible interest rate. When I say "lowest possible interest rate" I do not wish to imply subsidization of this type of financial activity. I believe, of course, that the loan should pay for itself; that the necessary administrative costs, and so forth, should be provided by the interest rate. Because exceptionally longterm financing is required, there is a necessity to keep the interest rate as low as possible. This the farm loan board has endeavoured to do. When it was originally established it did fix the initial interest rate considerably below the going rate of funds available from other sources, particularly from private sources.
Another principle that has to be kept in mind in regard to farm credit is the need for flexible repayment. Again, this uncertainty of income, this fluctuating income, which certainly we have had brought home to us quite forcibly during this present session, places the farmer in a position where he never knows from one year to another whether he is going to be able to meet his current liabilities. If he is not in a position where he can feel fairly secure concerning his credit operations, then of course he shows a great deal of reluctance to finance on this basis.
The farmer, because of his unfortunate experiences in the past during successive boom and bust periods, is very suspicious of credit; yet, because he is operating a separate family farm unit, he requires a comparatively high percentage of capitalization. If he is going to operate successfully he must use considerable amounts of capital. These
Canadian Farm Loan Act matters should all be kept in mind in reference to the provisions of this act now before us.
As I said at the beginning, the amendments are a step in the right direction, but there are still grounds for maintaining that the act has not moved as far as necessary, particularly when we consider the tremendous changes that have taken place in the farm economy since the act was originally placed on the statute books.
There are two more points I would like to make before I conclude my contribution to this discussion, Mr. Speaker. There are two types of credit need that have not been met in any shape or form by any type of capital operation in Canada up to the present time. The first is the special need that arises where the farmer finds himself operating an uneconomic unit. The main reason that his farm is regarded as an uneconomic unit, or is undercapitalized if you prefer that term, is because it is not large enough and is not fertile enough to bring sufficient return to provide a satisfactory income and living. Obviously, if he is going to change his farming operation into an economic one he has to obtain credit from some source in order to improve his position. Here is just where he finds himself up against a brick wall, because there is no possible source of credit. Private lenders, of course, turn him down flat; also, he is unable to get any assistance from either the Canadian Farm Loan Act or the Farm Improvement Loans Act.
' I have come up against specific examples of this sort of problem in my own area. A young farmer, for example, finds himself occupying a large expanse of territory which is semi-arid, submarginal and suitable mostly for grazing purposes. He is not in a position to buy the necessary cattle to turn his farming operation into an economic one. He is turned down by the Farm Improvement Loans Act and also by the farm loan board on the basis of the 60 per cent value stipulation, which, in the present amendment, has been changed to 65 per cent. That is a problem that must be faced in meeting the needs of the farm economy. Whether it can be done through the existing acts or whether it requires a broader approach to the problem I am not in a position to say, but certainly it requires some further study.
Then in this day and age, when farming has become a commercial operation, there is a special need of assistance for young farmers who are attempting to get started in farming operations. There is limited assistance under the Veterans Land Act so far as veterans are concerned and young farmers who can come under that act are assisted most generously

Canadian Farm Loan Act in getting established. However, outside of that particular program there is no adequate provision for credit assistance for the younger farmer wishing to get started.
I have some figures which indicate how the financial situation has changed in the last half century. In 1882 when western Canada was first opened up to homesteading a homesteader could get into business with an investment of some $660, and within five years he could have parlayed that original investment into something like $3,320. Today in order for a young farmer to be successfully launched the following minimum amounts are required:
Land	 $13,500
Buildings		 8,956
Machinery	and	equipment	 8,469
Livestock		 1,580
Cash for first	year's	operation _____ 2,099

As the parliamentary assistant has indicated, provision for credit of this kind is available under the act, but it is limited to a maximum of $15,000. This is a problem which has been discussed in this house before, as well as in the legislatures, particularly of the provinces of western Canada. I believe two provinces have acted to provide some assistance in this regard, Ontario being one and Quebec the other. Up to the present time the western provinces have not gone beyond the discussion stage.
It is obvious that today there is a trend away from the farms. If we are going to encourage young Canadians to establish family-farm units there will have to be provision for much more generous credit than is available under the act as it stands. In recent years there has been an increase in the number of tenant farmers, and no doubt this arises from the difficulty the farmer faces in getting started today because of the almost fantastic rise in the cost of farm operations. No doubt it also accounts for the rapid exodus from the farms to more lucrative occupations in the cities and urban areas.
Perhaps what we need is not an amendment to the act but a separate act which could be described as the farmers' establishment loan act. Or as an alternative the farm loan act could have a special division to be described as the farmers' establishment loan division. However, on the whole I think this bill is a step in the right direction, and I trust that any remarks I have made as to improvements that are required will be kept in mind when the amended act goes into effect.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) I welcome the fact that the government has recognized the problem

of agricultural credit, but I am disappointed that it is moving to resolve that problem at such a snail's pace. The problem of agricultural credit is particularly serious in Canada at the present time when agriculture is receiving such a small share of the national income, when we have a period such as last year when agriculture received only 6-8 per cent of the national income. This points up the necessity for the establishment of an overall agricultural credit policy to assist farmers in increasing their efficiency in order to offset the rising costs of production.
Agricultural credit is a serious problem in Canada at this time because of the transition which is taking place in many of our areas. In western Canada we have experienced a move toward larger farms, and we notice that the size of the farm is increased according to the efficiency of the equipment. That same move is taking place in Ontario, Quebec and the maritimes, indeed all across Canada. The size of the farm is co-ordinated with the efficiency of the farm machines which are being developed.
It is particularly important that we have a sound over-all agricultural credit policy to provide an opportunity to those of succeeding generations, who are desirous of taking up the occupation of farming, to take over the farms which their fathers have established on a sound and businesslike basis. As the hon. member for Brandon-Souris pointed out, in most instances the cost of becoming established is so prohibitive that unless assistance is provided by the father or by some magnanimous credit agency the young farmer is unable to become established. In many cases land which would become available as a family farm unit is absorbed by some other farm operator in the district who does not require it for the sake of efficiency but merely because he has a habit of acquiring more land.
We require an agricultural credit policy which will provide short-term, interim and long-term credit arrangements. As the parliamentary assistant pointed out, the Farm Improvement Loans Act is performing a most useful function in providing interim credit to farmers for the purchase of farm machinery, livestock and so on to ensure the maximum efficiency of their farms. I do not think we can say that the Canadian farm loan board has been achieving that same efficiency as a long-term credit organization.
The bill which is presently being discussed increases the percentage of the appraised value upon which a first mortgage can be granted. The parliamentary assistant has pointed out that this percentage is being increased from 60 to 65. At the same time the

maximum loan for a first and second mortgage is being increased from $12,000 to $15,000.
I had hoped at the time the resolution was introduced that the bill would include more than it has included, because it is necessary for this long-term credit policy to provide legislation that will achieve the function of establishing farmers on a sound basis in the agricultural industry of our economy.
The present Canadian Farm Loan Act has taken a very niggardly approach to giving credit to farmers for the avowed purpose of increasing the efficiency of the farm. Indeed, the total loans made have never approached the limit set for the board. The highest amount of outstanding Canadian farm loan board loans has been $30 million, as compared with an allowable $90 million. In 1954 this loan amount stood at $25 [DOT] 3 million, which indicates that the legislation does not encourage farmers to take advantage of this credit because of various defects in the Canadian Farm Loan Act.
One of the reasons would be, I think, the small margin upon which the board has to operate. Because of this small margin there is a very strong tendency to avoid making loans to high risk borrowers. In other words, if the farmer is in a hazardous position, if his farming operation does not appear to be an economic unit, the farm loan board is very reluctant to make him a loan so he can increase the efficiency of his unit.
I think another feature is the inadequate field staff with which the Canadian farm loan board has to operate. This is another indication of the operation of the Canadian farm loan board in trying to keep down expenses, whereas in effect it results in reductions in the loans that are actually made. There is an extensive delay in making appraisals. Because of the time element involved, there are many farmers that have not had an opportunity to purchase land, simply as a result of this delay.
I think the size of the loan as it stood before this amendment, $12,000, and the present $15,000, is still far too small. It is a small part of the actual purchase price for most farms. In addition to that, the board evaluations have in most instances been a half or less of market prices. The board has been very conservative in its appraisals, and has not given any recognition to the increase in land values that has taken place over the past number of years. The very fact that the percentage of the appraised value has been raised from 60 to 65 per cent is an indication of the fact that the appraised values have been far too low.
Another reason there have not been more loans made under the act would be the fact
Canadian Farm Loan Act that for a second mortgage a chattel mortgage is required on the livestock and assets of the farmer. This, in effect, ties up all the farmer's assets and puts him in an impossible position to get any further credit from any source whatsoever. Then in addition-

As the hon. member for Brandon-Souris pointed out, the terms of repayment under the Canadian Farm Loan Act are altogether too rigid. The fact that the repayment must be made in a period of 25 years by annual payments, with of course the option to prepay, does not take into consideration the weather cycles that periodically confront western Canada and, indeed, the whole of Canada. We need to have a flexible repayment policy that is geared to the average returns from the farm. By that I mean that, if a farmer has a good year, he should be expected to pay more to retire his debt. On the other hand, if he has a crop failure consideration should be given to that, and he should not be expected to pay any significant amount in that year.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture is certainly indebted to Mr. J. C. Brodrick, of St. Catharines, Ontario, for the investigation he has made into the need for agricultural credit in Canada. The house is doubtless aware of the recommendations made by the federation of agriculture pointing out the necessity for lengthening the period of repayment of the loans, increasing the maximum to $20,000, and changing the maximum assessment percentage to 80 per cent of loans up to $8,000, with a graduated reduction on the balance up to $20,000. The very fact that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture has had a discussion on this and has brought forth a comprehensive resolution on the necessity for an agricultural credit policy would certainly highlight the need for the establishment of an over-all credit policy for Canada.
I would suggest that we have a very good pattern to follow in establishing a long-term agricultural credit policy. I am one of those who are operating under the Veterans Land Act, and I must say that I have been most satisfied with the operation of that act. It takes into consideration the individual capacity of the settler and, through guidance and through a flexible repayment policy at a very low rate of interest, gives him every opportunity to establish himself.

I should like to see the government go one step further and study the policy which has been in effect for some time in the United States. I am thinking of the farmers' home administration, which was set up in 1939 and modified in 1946. The administration receives its funds by annual appropriation from the government. The loans are made to those who have a good chance of succeeding if given assistance. The attitude is taken that the most important asset of the farm is the farmer, and if he is willing to work and has the ability and the guidance, there is every possible chance that he will succeed.
Loans are made on 100 per cent of the appraised value of a farm. They do not believe in going half way. They will give a farmer assistance on the basis of an economic unit and will fix up the farm home. Indeed, it is one of the provisos of the farmers' home administration that the farm must be established as an economic unit and one fit to be inhabited. In fact there was one instance in the United States where the farmers' home administration took over a farm to set up a bankrupt individual and get him back on his feet. They of course insisted that he build a new, modern home to house his wife and children, and of course funds were supplied for that purpose. The interesting aspect there is that the house he had been occupying had to be improved in order to be fit to house hogs.
They believe in going at things in a reasonable fashion so the farmer has every possible chance to succeed. They have a flexible repayment policy which, as I indicated, should be incorporated in this legislation so that if the farmer has the finances to repay the loan in any particular year he would be encouraged to do so.
He should also be given all possible assistance through agricultural research and by way of receiving the advice of officials having to do with the administration of the act so that he may be an efficient operator. You can see, Mr. Speaker, that there is a big field open with respect to this whole subject of agricultural credit. Many improvements can be made and are necessary in short-term, intermediate-term and long-term credit; and I suggest to the parliamentary assistant that the best way for this to be brought about is to refer the bill to the standing committee on agriculture for thorough study. It should be referred to the committee so those interested farm organizations such as the Canadian Federation of Agriculture who have discussed this matter, may have the opportunity to present their views in order that the bill may 

be revised in such a way as to provide a
dynamic source of agricultural credit which
is so needed in Canada today.

Just one minute; I am going to bring that out. I noticed that a few years ago the ceiling was $5,000. It was increased to $10,000 and now it is anticipated that the maximum ceiling will be $15,000. I have mentioned that this is good but not good enough. I also note that throughout the years there have been changes in the percentage of money lent on the appraised valuation of the property concerned.
I notice that the amount has been increased from 50 per cent to 60 per cent and now to 65 per cent. We are prepared to give credit where credit is due, Mr. Speaker, but we will give just as much credit as is due and no more. We do not feel that the legislation is perfect in any way yet, and for this reason we should like to see further amendments.
I am particularly interested in the problem of the young man who wishes to take up farming. Some years ago a man could go out west, take up a homestead for $10, buy a team of horses, a sulky plow, a hayrack and so on for a few more hundred dollars and become established. That day is long past, and as we go down through the years we find that it has become ever more costly for a man to establish himself upon a farm. In fact in my part of the province of Alberta it would cost a minimum of $20,000 today for a young man to become established, and that not on the best grade of land in that part of the province but on average land.

That is a lot of money for a young man to have to pay to become established as a farmer.
We must remember that after he has paid $20,000 for the land he has to buy a full line of machinery. If he is engaged in mixed farming he has to go into cattle and so on. This is a costly investment, and for that reason I wish to submit, with all due respect to what has been done in the past, that a ceiling of $15,000 is far too low. I have here a copy of an application that one of my constituents submitted to the Canadian farm loan board. He was trying to borrow $10,000. It so happened that last summer he visited the branch office and met the man in charge at this particular point. He explained his case and was told that he did not have sufficient security for the board to grant him a loan of $10,000. One of the reasons advanced, of course, was that he did not have enough cultivated acreage.
I am thinking in terms of a farm of five quarter-sections of land. On these five quarter sections there were, according to this man's statement, 460 acres under cultivation. At that time the man had 50 head of cattle. Those of us who are acquainted with farming in the west will realize that it takes a goodly amount of pasture to feed the cattle through the summer and to have feed for them throughout the winter. He not only had 50 head of cattle but had 50 head of hogs; he was in the hog business as well. He had a full line of machinery, and an approximate estimate of the net value of the property he owned at that time would be $27,500. Nevertheless he was refused.

The farm loan board provides only a relatively small proportion of the mortgage credit in this country-perhaps 15 per cent of the total.
This is interesting, Mr. Speaker, in view of the remarks made by my good friend the hon. member for Brandon-Souris.
Its lending policies are conservative, and its own financial policies are also very conservative.

I did not expect that influence from the present government.
I have also mentioned the fact that on the part of the officials of the Canadian farm loan board little or no attempt is made to sell the product they have; and the product they have is the authority to make loans available to the farmers and the fishermen of Canada when they are necessary. I would also mention the cumbersome type of application form used by the present Canadian farm loan board. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that there is only one other form, to my knowledge, that is any more complicated than this one, and it is the form the farmer must fill out when he files his income tax.
I believe that the man who drafted this form must also have drafted its sister form, the farmer's income tax form. I believe it would take an exceptionally good lawyer to satisfy the directors of the Canadian farm loan board that these questions were answered properly.
Then there is the matter of appraisement. Just what is wrong with the present system of appraisement? In the particular case I have mentioned no appraisal was made, of course; there was just an offhand statement, "No, you don't get it". There was no attempt to find out whether or not the statements which this young man submitted were correct. When a man drives in from the country to the city and makes a personal application for a loan, surely the least we should expect from the farm loan board is a survey or investigation, through the municipal officials or some other body, to find out as a preliminary whether or not the figures submitted by this particular farmer were fair, honest and so on.
