speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to say a few words in this debate I should first like to congratulate the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance on the clear and concise report he gave with respect to the amendment to this act. Since his presentation I have listened with interest to the remarks made by the

hon. member for Brandon-Souris the hon. member for Kindersley and the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose.
Dealing with the last first, I would say that the hon. member devoted most of his remarks to a criticism of one special case which had come to his notice. Dealing next with the hon. member for Kindersley, I would say he commended the government on a special case, and that was his own. Going back to the first, I listened to the remarks of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris but I cannot really admit that he contributed too much to this debate. It seemed to me that his thinking was along the same lines he exhibited the other evening when he attempted to cure the ills of the maritime provinces on the decentralization problem by telling us we should go back to the policies introduced by the Conservative party at the time of confederation.
I would come now to the bill itself Mr. Speaker. I would say that I agree entirely with the principle of this bill, but I do not entirely agree with the application of its principle to date. At its annual meeting held in Truro in January of this year, the Nova Scotia federation of agriculture passed the following resolution under the heading of "Farm Credit Policy":
Whereas our present credit facilities are not adequate to meet the requirements of an expanding industry in a way that producers may increase their production units to a profitable and efficient level.
Resolved that provincial and federal authorities make every effort to expand all types of farm credit policy.
I am very hopeful, Mr. Speaker, that the amendment to this bill is carrying out the policy advocated. Perhaps those of you who are interested in the problems of Nova Scotia will recall that our provincial legislature has set up a royal commission to study all phases of agriculture credit. I would say that is a step in the right direction.
Now, sir, perhaps some of you will say to me, what right has a member from Nova Scotia to participate in an agriculture debate? I should like to state here that Nova Scotia, small as it is, has a farm population of
112.000,	according to the census of 1951, compared with a farm population in Canada of
2.827.000.	In other words Nova Scotia, in spite of all that has happened in the past, still has 4 per cent of the farm population of Canada.
I am going to deal now more specifically with the workings of the Canadian Farm Loan Act in Nova Scotia. In trying to lead up to this I placed a question on the order paper as far back as February 13 requesting a breakdown of the farm loans granted and
Canadian Farm Loan Act applied for in Nova Scotia during the last calendar year. I might say that my reason for doing this was based on that resolution passed by the Nova Scotia federation of agriculture previously referred to. I was afraid that the Canadian farm loan board had forgotten there was any agriculture in Nova Scotia. As yet I have not received a reply to this question, so in dealing with this problem I must base my remarks on the last annual report of the Canadian farm loan board, for the year ending March 31, 1955.
As I have said, Nova Scotia has 4 per cent of the farm population of Canada; yet according to the figures in the annual report, at March 31, 1955, Nova Scotia had 3-4 per cent of the farm loans outstanding as compared with the rest of Canada. I am coming now to the application of the farm loan program in Nova Scotia in the last year. I want to again impress the fact upon you that Nova Scotia has 4 per cent of the farm population of Canada. According to this report, in the last year Nova Scotia was given only 1-2 per cent of the farm loans which were made, that is according to number, and according to amount we fared even worse because we got only 1-07 per cent of the loans.
In view of those figures, and in view of the fact I have not been able to get an answer to the question I asked concerning loans made in the calendar year, I find myself in the position where I must agree with the criticism which was raised at the annual meeting of the Nova Scotia federation of agriculture. They said that the Canadian farm loan board had lost interest in the farmers of that province.
Where is the parliamentary assistant? I hope he will follow me when I say that I trust this new program will mean the farmers of Nova Scotia will not be forgotten. I have given you the figures showing what we have had. Our farmers think this is a great plan if it is properly applied but they cannot see that, on the percentage of loans granted under the present scheme, they are being properly treated.
The farm loan board maintains an office in Halifax, the capital of Nova Scotia. With all respect to my good friends from Halifax, I would say that Halifax is not in touch with the rural portions of the province because it is so far away. Last year this loan office granted to the farmers of Nova Scotia 31 loans totalling $88,750. I might say in all sincerity that if a farmer loan organization in Nova Scotia, where there are 112,000 farm people and with all the applications they have had, cannot put out more money than that, then either agriculture in Nova Scotia is doomed or the farm loan board is not doing its duty.

Canadian Farm Loan Act
Let me go back a bit. A few years ago it was my privilege to sit in this house, and it still is. With all respect to my good friends from Halifax-the war was on and Halifax was carrying the load for Canada, as every Nova Scotian did, but Halifax bore the brunt of it-I advocated that the place for the Canadian farm loan board was in the centre of agricultural production in Nova Scotia, not away out on the headland with the shipping, which had very little connection with agriculture. Although I made my point, it was indicated to me at that time that in addition to administering the Canadian farm loan, the farm loan board had to look after fishermen's loans. There was nothing I could say to offset that, because farming and fishing in the interior of Nova Scotia had nothing in common.
In view of the remarks of the parliamentary assistant I now find, sir,-and I am now saying this to the parliamentary assistant and through him to the Minister of Finance- that the terrific job the Canadian farm loan board had to do to look after loans to fishermen in Nova Scotia was to make four loans to the total of $1,291.11. Because of this new outlook on farm loan advances, I hope the rural people of Nova Scotia will be able to get a proper office in the centre of the province.
In addition to the improvement in the farm loan board administration, I hope the board will put its offices in the centre of the farming population where they will be in close contact with our farming problems. Why should the Canadian farm loan board, lending money to the farmers of Nova Scotia, be
located where it is? Halifax is a wonderful city, but on the other hand the federal Department of Agriculture has its main offices in the constituency of Colchester-Hants. The Veterans Land Act, which lends money to put people on the land, has an office there, and the Nova Scotia government in all its wisdom-and it is a good government-has the agricultural college at Truro. The headquarters of all their agricultural activities is there. If I could only impress upon our federal people, if they are to play a real role and do a decent job for the farmers of Nova Scotia, the necessity of bringing their activities to the farmers rather than have the farmers going to them, it would be a great day for the farm loan board, for the Minister of Finance, for his parliamentary assistant, and for the member for Colchester-Hants.
Thank you very much.
